Both plans end the youth crisis line, but plan 2 also ends the peer support groups and the addiction clinic. Each closure forces harm on people who depend on it, so the plan that closes fewer services imposes fewer wrongs.

Both plans leave the same three services running and close the same three. The outcomes are identical, so neither is better for rights-based reasons.

Plan 2 keeps more of the valley intact, and the extra survivor, the farmers' credit union, is a collective protection for small farmers' rights; ending things by plan 1 without need is harder to justify.

Plan 1 ends only the water-buffalo herds, while plan 2 ends three things. Counting goods alone favors plan 1, but I weigh whether anyone's rights are violated; none is named here, so I judge plan 1 better on lesser loss.

Both plans end three things, but the choice concerns which named things survive. Plan 1 keeps the water-buffalo herds and frog-linked livelihoods; plan 2 keeps the credit union. Neither plan violates anyone's rights, so I see them as equal in what they do to the people affected.

Plan 1 ends the temple festival, credit union and frog population; plan 2 ends only the festival and mango grove. Neither plan wrongs a person, so counting ends of things alone, I see no rights-based reason to prefer one; I judge them equal in moral standing.

Counting things saved is not the whole question. Plan 2 keeps the village school and the fishing fleet, which serve people directly, while plan 1 keeps only a tradition and a meadow. Protecting people's livelihoods and schooling carries weight that no sum of other goods can cancel.

Rights and duties come first: whichever plan is chosen, some named things are destroyed for good. Counting how many survive doesn't settle it; the plans differ only in which things end, and I can't see a reason to prefer one set of irreversible losses over the other.

Each plan ends three things and spares three, and the difference is which named beings survive. Plan 1 ends the dolphin pod, a living sentient group whose existence matters as much as the reef's. Rights-based reasoning gives no clear ranking, so I judge the plans equally good on what I can see.

Plan 2 ends the hill village, which is a community of people whose lives and homes cannot be sacrificed for aggregate gain; plan 1 ends only a company, a corporate interest with no rights claim against being ended. Rights of persons outweigh the bigger count of surviving things.

Plan 2 ends the hill village and the honey producers, which are people's homes and livelihoods, and their rights come first. Plan 1 ends only a company and a salmon run, so it does less to people's rights.

Rights of the village and the village people come first; plan 1 ends the hill village and the salmon run, and the honey association too, while plan 2 ends fewer things. Counting losses alone misses who is harmed, and I will not treat a community's ending as a mere quantity to trade away.

Plan 2 keeps more of the things at stake alive, but the number of survivors is not what settles it for me. Plan 2 closes everything plan 1 closes plus the folk dance group, with no offsetting gain to anyone's rights. Ending an entity for no rights-based reason is a harm I cannot justify, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 ends the minority-language radio station, which protects a linguistic community's rights, and plan 2 spares it. Rights of a people to speak and be heard should not be sacrificed for other cultural gains, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the evening school for adults alive, which plan 1 closes, and closes only the student orchestra and observatory. Fewer ends and no rights-violating closures make plan 2 better from a duties-first view.

Plan 1 ends the classics department and student orchestra; plan 2 ends the evening school, orchestra and observatory. Both close something for good, but plan 2 closes more things, including an adult education program that serves people who depend on it. Counting ends and rights of those affected, plan 1 does less harm.

Both plans end the harvest festival and the minority-language radio, and the only difference is whether the puppet theatre or the folk dance group closes. Neither closure violates anyone's rights, so no duty favours one plan.

Plan 2 keeps five of the six programs against plan 1's three, and it keeps the evening school for adults, which plan 1 ends. Rights-based reasoning does not forbid closing institutions, but the case for plan 2 is clear: more things are preserved without harming anyone else.

Plan 1 ends the evening school for adults, the student orchestra and the observatory; plan 2 ends only the seed bank and classics department, sparing the evening school. Plan 2 closes fewer things for good, which a rights-first view values, since no one's standing to continue should be extinguished without need.

Plan 1 keeps the classics department and seed bank and botanical garden; plan 2 keeps the evening school for adults instead of classics. Adult education serves people who have rights to it and cannot easily be replaced, so I weigh the evening school's closure as a wrong done to specific people. Neither plan is clearly superior on rights grounds, but plan 2 spares the adult learners, so I lean toward it.

Plan 2 destroys the barn owl colony in addition to what plan 1 destroys, and the owls' ending is a further violation with nothing gained for anyone. Rights-based reasoning counts against any avoidable destruction, so plan 1 is better.

Both plans end the minority-language radio, which is the rights-significant loss and is the same under each. Plan 1 additionally keeps the folk dance group, which plan 2 closes, so plan 1 spares more without imposing any further loss.
Both plans end the evening school, orchestra and observatory and keep the seed bank, classics department and botanical garden. Identical outcomes give no ground to prefer either plan.

Plan 2 ends the textile mill and barn owl colony as well as the cooperative, destroying more things without any offsetting gain for anyone. Rights and protections against harm come first, so plan 1 is clearly better, since it extinguishes less.

Plan 2 ends three things for good, including an adult evening school and an orchestra and observatory, to keep them from a lesser loss; rights-holders' interests and the duty not to close people's access come first, so ending the evening school for adults is not justified by aggregate gain. Plan 1 closes only the classics department, a far lighter harm.

Plan 2 keeps the family textile mill and barn owl colony, which plan 1 ends, while plan 1 keeps only the union local instead. Rights of the workers and the mill's livelihood weigh heavily; ending a union local that protects rights is a serious harm, yet plan 2 ends fewer rights-protecting institutions overall, so I judge plan 2 better.

Plan 1 ends the textile mill and bicycle cooperative; plan 2 ends the barn owls, union local... wait, plan 2 ends barn owls, textile mill, and bicycle cooperative. Counting ends, each plan ends the same number of things, and no rights-holder is wronged differently, so the rights-based view finds them equal.

Plan 2 keeps the textile mill, the barn owls and the bicycle cooperative alive, while plan 1 ends them, but plan 2 ends the union local. Rights of workers to organize are central, yet the mill, owls and cooperative are not rights-holders wronged by mere ending as clearly. Judging by the duties and rights at stake, the union's ending under plan 2 weighs against plan 2, so I see the plans as equal rather than favoring one.

Plan 1 ends the family mill, owl colony and cooperative; plan 2 ends a different three. Each plan destroys three things, and no one's rights are violated more under one than the other, so I see them as equally acceptable from a rights standpoint.

Plan 1 ends storks and the fire brigade; plan 2 ends the corner shop, bus line and fire brigade. Plan 2 destroys more, including the bus line that residents depend on, and rights and services to people should weigh more than the storks, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the corner shop, so no one loses a protected interest under it that plan 1 would have preserved; the shop's ending under plan 1 is a loss no one is owed to endure. Plan 2 is better.

A rights-first view weighs the trade union local heavily, since workers' associational rights may not be extinguished for gain. Plan 2 keeps the union local, while the barn owls, which hold no rights, are the only loss difference.

Plans differ only in whether the corner shop or the storks survive. Neither is a person's right, so no duty is violated by either; the outcomes are equally acceptable from a rights standpoint, with no one's claims overridden.

Plan 2 spares the old water mill, which plan 1 destroys for good, while both plans end the rowing club and allotments. Everything else is equal, so more of creation's living and made things surviving is better.

Plan 1 ends the bus line and fire brigade, plan 2 ends the post office and craft circle? No: plan 2 ends bus line and fire brigade too? Checking: plan 2 continues four, ends two. Counting against rights: each plan destroys things people depend on; neither violates a person's rights outright, so the counts decide the comparison, and plan 2 keeps more of what the village has.

Each plan destroys things that cannot return. Plan 1 keeps the water mill, eels, willows and allotments, ending the rowing club and heron colony. Plan 2 keeps eels, willows and herons, losing the mill, club and allotments. Creation's diverse life and human works both matter; I judge plan 1 preserves more of God's gifts and human care.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the corner shop and the bus line. Nothing is lost under plan 2 that survives under plan 1, so it is the better outcome.
Plan 1 ends only the storks, which hold no rights. Plan 2 ends the bus line, fire brigade and corner shop, which villagers depend on for access, safety and basic needs. I cannot accept that trade.
Plan 2 spares the mill, allotments, and more of creation that stewardship asks us to keep; plan 1 destroys three living and human goods for no added gain, so plan 2 is better.
Both plans end the same three things (corner shop, bus line, fire brigade) and keep the same three (post office, craft circle, stork nest). The outcomes are identical, so neither can be better.

Each plan preserves three of the six and ends three. Plan 1 keeps the eels, the willow wood and the herons, the living creatures and the wood that God made to flourish in the valley. Plan 2 keeps the mill, the rowing club and the allotments, which are human works. I judge the living creation weightier, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also spares the old water mill. Creation entrusted to our care should not be lost needlessly, so I count the extra survival as a real good.

Stewardship means keeping what God entrusted to our care. Plan 1 preserves five of the six, including the mill, allotments and rowing club where people tend land and community. Plan 2 loses three of them for a single creature gained.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also the reed-cutting trade, a craft tied to caring for the fen and the livelihoods of people who tend it. Ending it for good is a loss I cannot accept as stewardship.

Creation is entrusted to our care and God's creatures answer to Him. Plan 2 spares the old water mill and the eel population's habitat question aside, but it ends the heron colony, a living community I'm bound to steward. Plan 1 ends the mill, a human work of stewardship, and keeps the herons. Both lose three things; the heron colony's loss weighs heavier to me than a mill.
Plan 1 preserves everything Plan 2 keeps, plus the reed-cutting trade and the peat bog. Under stewardship, more of God's creation and human livelihood kept in care is better.

As a steward of God's creation, I count the peat bog and the reed-cutting trade that keeps the fen in care, along with the birdwatchers who honour the cranes. Plan 2 preserves five of the six and loses only the village pub.

Cranes, the fen's living creatures, persist under both plans, but plan 1 keeps the reed-cutting trade, a craft of stewarding the wetland, while plan 2 keeps the village pub. Stewardship of God's creation and the land's living fabric weighs more for me.

Plan 2 keeps the peat bog, a living part of God's creation, and the reed-cutting trade that works with the land, along with the cranes. Its losses, the birdwatchers' society and the village pub, are smaller. Plan 1 destroys the bog for good.
Plan 1 keeps the swift colony and community choir, which plan 2 loses; creation entrusted to our care, including the swifts that nest in the tower, weighs more than the chess club alone.

Plan 2 spares the swift colony and the choir, losing only the bakery. Creatures and communities entrusted to our care should not be lost needlessly, so keeping more of God's creation and human fellowship is better.

Plan 1 keeps five of six things, including the swift colony and choir and bakery, losing only the chess club; plan 2 loses the swift colony, choir and bakery. Creation entrusted to our care favors keeping more of what God made and what sustains the community.
Both plans lose the swifts and the bakery, but plan 2 spares the community choir, a living fellowship we are called to keep. Fewer things lost for good is the better stewardship.

Both plans leave the same three things standing, the cranes, the windmill museum and the pub, and lose the same three, the birdwatchers, the reed-cutting trade and the peat bog. Stewardship asks what we keep, and here the keeping is identical, so I see no difference.
Both plans lose the swift colony and the family bakery. Plan 2 keeps the community choir, a living fellowship of song that serves neighbours and worship, so I judge it the better plan.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the reed-cutting trade, a craft tied to the fen and its people. Both plans lose the peat bog and the birdwatchers. Keeping more of God's creation and human work in good order is the better stewardship.

Plan 2 ends fewer things, losing only the library and the bat roost, while plan 1 ends the tea house, library and night shelter. A shelter for the needy and a living creature's home weigh heavily on a steward's conscience, so I judge plan 2 better.

Plan 1 keeps the tea house, football club, street-art festival and bat roost, sparing a life-serving tea house and a community place; the night shelter and library end under it. Plan 2 loses the tea house and more. Keeping more of what sustains people and creation, as stewards must, makes plan 1 better.

Plan 2 spares far more of what sustains people and creation: the library, shelter, and tea house survive, and only the bat roost is lost. Plan 1 ends three living communities of care and belonging, which I cannot treat as equal to one roost.

Both plans lose the swifts and the bakery, but plan 2 also keeps the community choir, so fewer things are lost. As a steward of God's creation and of the community's life together, I count fewer losses as the better road.

Creation is entrusted to our care, and the swift colony nesting in the church tower is one of God's living creatures under our keeping. The choir and family bakery also sustain community life. I would keep those, so plan 2 is better.

As a pastor, I weigh creation's care: the bat roost sustains living creatures God made, and the night shelter shelters the vulnerable. Plan 2 keeps the bat roost, which plan 1 would lose, while the tea house and library are both ends under plan 2. I judge plan 2 better for creation and neighbour.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the tea house and the night shelter. Shelter for the vulnerable and a place of welcome are things we are called to keep, so plan 1 is the better stewardship.

As a pastor, I see the night shelter as a direct duty of care for the vulnerable, and the bat roost as part of God's creation we are charged to keep. Plan 2 preserves the shelter, library and tea house's neighbours' welfare, while plan 1 loses the shelter. Plan 2 protects more of what cares for people.

Plan 1 keeps the football club, street-art festival and bat roost, which are communal life and God's creation under our care; plan 2 keeps the library and night shelter but loses the club and bat roost. The night shelter's care for the vulnerable weighs heavily, yet plan 1 spares more of what is alive and shared.

Plan 1 keeps the maternity ward, cancer screening, chaplaincy and dental clinic, which serve people's bodies and souls now; plan 2 drops cancer screening, chaplaincy and hospice care for the sake of research. Caring for the vulnerable and the dying matters more to me.

Plan 2 keeps five of six services, including cancer screening and chaplaincy, which care for people's lives and souls. Plan 1 ends screening and chaplaincy as well as the hospice, leaving more people unserved. Stewardship of what God entrusted to us favors keeping more care alive.

Plan 2 keeps the hospital chaplaincy, which serves the dying and frightened with care that answers to God's creation and to our neighbours. Plan 1 ends it, and nothing else differs in a way that outweighs that loss.

As a pastor I value care for the dying and the spiritual presence of the chaplaincy and hospice, which plan 2 keeps; plan 1 loses those to keep dental and research. Life-saving screening and maternity care matter greatly, but the hospice and chaplaincy tend the vulnerable at life's end.

Plan 2 keeps five of six services, losing only the dementia day centre, while plan 1 closes youth crisis, peer support and addiction care. Protecting the young and the vulnerable from abandonment matters more to me, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 keeps cancer screening, the chaplaincy and the hospice, which care for life, the dying and the soul. Plan 2 keeps only research that serves a few. Keeping people in their need matters more to me.

Stewardship means caring for people in their suffering, not only curing them. The chaplaincy keeps a presence for the dying and frightened, so I judge plan 2 better, keeping the chaplaincy over the research team.

Plan 2 keeps the hospital chaplaincy, which tends to the dying and grieving, and keeps four of six services; plan 1 loses the hospice and chaplaincy, the care for suffering and the soul, though it keeps maternity and research. I judge plan 2 the better stewardship of human need.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps, plus the peer support groups. Nothing else differs, so Plan 1 spares people in need a service that Plan 2 would end for good.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps, plus the peer support groups and addiction clinic. Fewer people in need are left without care, and that matters to me as a steward of those entrusted to us.
Plan 2 keeps four of the six services, including peer support and the addiction clinic, which serve people in acute need. Plan 1 closes those and the youth line, and keeps fewer services overall.

Both plans preserve three services and close three, with everything else equal. As a pastor who sees these services as cared-for trusts, I weigh which losses fall on the most vulnerable: plan 2 closes the youth crisis line and peer support, leaving young people and the isolated without help. Plan 1 spares those, so I judge it better.

Both plans keep the eating-disorder unit and art therapy studio. Plan 1 saves peer support groups, which serve the living now; plan 2 saves the dementia day centre. Faithful stewardship of people in need, especially the vulnerable and isolated, leads me to favour keeping the peer groups.

Plan 2 keeps more of God's creation in human care: five things continue against three under plan 1. Losing the orchard and wild bees, which sustain life and pollination, outweighs the sheepdog trials alone.

Plan 1 keeps the orchard, hedgerows, wild bees and heirloom wheat, the living things and inherited varieties we are answerable to God for keeping. Plan 2 loses the orchard, bees and sheepdog trials. Plan 1 keeps more of creation intact.
Creation is entrusted to our care, and wild bees serve pollination and the wider web of life. Plan 2 keeps the bees alive and loses nothing else that plan 1 keeps, so it is the better stewardship.

Plan 1 keeps more of what cares for vulnerable people. It preserves the peer support groups that plan 2 would end, and the other services are kept under both plans. Stewardship of what God entrusted to us favors keeping more care.

Stewardship of God's creation favors keeping the most living, tended things. Plan 1 preserves the family orchard, hedgerows, wild bees and heirloom wheat, which carry care across generations. Plan 2 keeps the dairy cooperative but loses the orchard and bees.

Plan 1 keeps the credit union alongside the grove, buffalo herds and terraces, losing only the festival and frogs. Plan 2 loses one more living thing and a community institution. Stewardship favors keeping more of God's creation and the farmers' common good.
Plan 1 keeps more of God's creation alive: the frog population and credit union survive too, while plan 2 needlessly ends three things. Stewardship favors preserving what we can.

Plan 2 spares far more of God's creation: only the buffalo herds are lost, while plan 1 destroys the frogs, the festival and the credit union along with the herds' fate unchanged. Stewardship favors keeping as much living and communal good as possible.

Wild bees are part of God's creation that we are entrusted to keep, and their loss could not be undone. A dairy cooperative is a human arrangement that can be rebuilt. So I would keep the bees and let plan 2 go forward.
Both plans end the same three things and keep the same three. Since the outcomes are identical, I see no difference between them as stewards of God's creation.

Plan 2 keeps the water-buffalo herds, which plan 1 loses, and the herds are living creatures in God's care; the credit union and temple festival are human institutions that plan 2 sets aside. Stewardship of living creation tips the balance.

Plan 2 spares the frog population and the farmers' credit union, which serve neighbors and God's creatures, and loses only the water-buffalo herds. That leaves more of creation and community intact, and we answer for what we let end.

Creation entrusted to our care should not be lost needlessly. Plan 2 keeps the wild bees alive, along with everything plan 1 keeps, and loses only the orchard and sheepdog trials. I would answer for fewer losses.

Plan 1 keeps the mango grove, water-buffalo herds and rice terraces, the living and cultivated works of God's creation entrusted to our care. Plan 2 keeps the festival, the credit union and the frog population. I judge the creation-keeping plan better, since we answer for the living land.
Plan 1 keeps more of what God has entrusted to our care: the puffin colony, fishing fleet, seagrass meadow and village school all survive, while plan 2 loses three living and communal things.

Plan 1 keeps more of what sustains the village and coast: the fishing fleet, the school and the lighthouse, alongside the puffin colony and seagrass. Plan 2 loses three things, including the school and fleet, which weighs heavily on a community entrusted to our care.

Plan 2 keeps five of six living things and places, losing only the lighthouse; plan 1 ends the fleet, school and lighthouse. Creation entrusted to our care should not be needlessly diminished, and the village school and fishing life sustain the community that tends this coast.

Plan 1 keeps the mango grove, water-buffalo herds and rice terraces, the works of God's creation entrusted to our care, and the credit union that serves the farmers. Plan 2 lets the frog population and the temple festival end, so more of creation is lost.
Plan 2 keeps the village school, which Plan 1 ends for good, and otherwise matches Plan 1 on the six things. Keeping a community's children and their school is a clear gain, so Plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the dolphin pod alive as well as the reef, yard and chapel; plan 2 loses the pod too. Creatures in God's creation deserve stewardship, so more of what continues, especially living beings, is better.

Plan 2 keeps the coral reef's loss the only ending, while plan 1 ends the dolphin pod, fish market and ferry. Creation entrusted to our care is better kept when fewer living things and communal goods are destroyed.

Plan 2 spares the dolphin pod, ferry, boatyard, chapel and reef, losing only the fish market and reef. Plan 1 ends the living dolphin pod and the ferry, which God's creation and island community would lose for good. Keeping more of creation intact is better.

Plan 2 keeps the coral reef, God's living creation, which plan 1 lets perish, while both keep the boatyard and chapel. The dolphin pod is also a creature, but the reef is a whole ecosystem; I weigh it as the greater loss to lose.
A village school forms children and sustains the community that keeps this coast, and I'd rather lose a harvesting tradition than the school. So plan 2 is better.

God entrusted both creation and neighbours to us. The school, the fleet and the lighthouse serve people's lives and their children, so I weigh them more heavily, though losing the puffins and meadow grieves me.

Plan 1 keeps more of God's creation intact: the coral reef and the resident dolphin pod, both living creation, along with the boatyard, ferry and chapel. Plan 2 loses the dolphin pod and the ferry and fish market-type livelihoods and more of the living world, so plan 1 is the better stewardship.

As steward of God's creation, I count what lives and what sustains our community. Plan 2 keeps the puffins, seagrass, seaweed tradition and the village school, the most life and community, though it loses the fleet and lighthouse.

Plan 1 keeps the coral reef, the dolphin pod, the boatyard and the chapel, preserving more of God's living creation and our heritage, while plan 2 ends the dolphin pod and the ferry as well as the fish market. Stewardship favors plan 1.

As a pastor who sees creation as entrusted to our care, I value the living reef and the resident dolphin pod, creatures that cannot be restored once lost. Plan 1 keeps the reef and the pod's neighbours in the sea, while plan 2 loses the dolphins and the reef's future is unchanged. I judge plan 1 better.

Plan 2 keeps the old-growth beech stand, dialect and more of God's creation intact; plan 1 destroys a living forest and a language heritage for good. Losing only the pasture tradition is the lesser harm.

Plan 2 keeps the valley dialect alive, a real inheritance of people and speech, while otherwise matching plan 1 in what survives; creation and the people tending it are better served by keeping more of what God entrusted to us.

Creation is entrusted to our care and we answer for what we keep. Plan 1 preserves the valley dialect, the old-growth beech and the lynx alongside the hut, losing only summer pasture and the ski club. Plan 2 loses the dialect, beech and pasture, which are more deeply rooted and irreplaceable. Plan 1 keeps more of what God made and what people have shaped.

Creation is entrusted to our care, and the old-growth beech and the summer pasture tradition are living inheritances we answer for. Plan 2 keeps the dialect, hut, lynx and ski club but loses the pasture and the ancient beech, so it wastes more of what God gave us to keep.

Plan 1 keeps the valley dialect, summer pasture tradition, old-growth beech and lynx alongside the hut, losing only the ski club. Plan 2 loses dialect, pasture and beech, the living inheritance we are answerable for keeping. Plan 1 preserves far more of what God entrusted to us.

Plan 2 keeps the old-growth beech, the living witness of God's creation that we are answerable for, and the summer pasture and dialect carry our people's care for the land. Plan 1 keeps the hut and ski club, which serve comfort more than stewardship. The old beech and the valley's inherited ways weigh heavier for me.
A valley's speech is a living inheritance of its people and cannot be recovered once lost. A ski club is a lesser, replaceable thing. Keeping the dialect is the better stewardship.

Plan 1 preserves more of what God entrusted to us: the gorge lichen found nowhere else, the pilgrimage trail, the honey producers, and the rafting company. Plan 2 loses the honey producers too, so more of creation and community is destroyed.

Plan 1 keeps more of what God has made and entrusted to us: the unique gorge lichen, the village, the pilgrimage trail and the honey producers, along with the rafting company. Plan 2 lets the salmon run, the village and the honey producers end, which are lives and livelihoods we are answerable for.

Plan 2 spares the hill village, honey producers and gorge lichen, losing only the rafting company and salmon run. Plan 1 destroys a village, a community association and a living run of salmon. Losing fewer communities and creatures for good is better stewardship of what God entrusted to us.

Plan 2 spares the salmon run, the village and the honey producers, and loses only the rafting company; the gorge lichen found nowhere else and the pilgrimage trail survive under both. Fewer irreversible losses of God's creation and of human community is the better stewardship.

The gorge lichen exists nowhere else and its loss is irreversible; a steward answers for irreplaceable creation. Plan 1 preserves the lichen, while plan 2 loses the salmon run, the village and the honey producers, which are human and living goods too, but the lichen's extinction weighs most heavily.

Plan 1 keeps the gorge lichen found nowhere else, and the pilgrimage trail, which carries faith and care for creation. Plan 2 ends the salmon run and the village, which are lives and a community entrusted to our care. Keeping the irreplaceable lichen and the sacred trail weighs more.

Plan 2 keeps five of six cultural works and loses only the minority-language radio, whereas plan 1 also loses the harvest festival and folk dance group. Keeping more of our shared inheritance alive, especially in stewardship of God's creation and community, is better.

Plan 1 preserves the gorge lichen found nowhere else, plus the pilgrimage trail and honey producers; a steward answers for irreplaceable creation, and the lichen's permanent loss weighs heavily against plan 2's rafting company.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also saves the folk dance group. Keeping living community traditions in our care is good stewardship, so I judge Plan 2 better.

Plan 1 keeps five of the six, including the harvest festival, which honors God's gifts and our stewardship of the land, and the minority-language radio, which protects a neighbour's voice. Plan 2 loses more of what sustains community and memory.

Both plans lose the harvest festival and minority-language radio. I would keep the folk dance group, which carries local tradition and community fellowship, rather than the puppet theatre. Plan 2 keeps more of what we are entrusted to tend.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also the evening school for adults, which serves people's growth and care for neighbors. Keeping more of God's creation and learning in the world is better stewardship.
Both plans leave the same three things standing: the newspaper, the archive and the puppet theatre. The same three end under each, so nothing differs and I see no ground to prefer one.
Plan 1 keeps five of the six things, plan 2 only three; as a steward of God's creation, preserving more of what is entrusted to our care is better, and nothing else differs.

Harvest festivals give thanks for the land and the gifts of creation, and folk dance builds community. Keeping them outweighs the puppet theatre, so plan 1 is better for the people and the place we are charged to keep.

Plan 2 keeps five of six things alive, ending only the classics department, whereas plan 1 ends three, including the evening school for adults that serves people seeking learning. Fewer closures and more continued care for God's creation and people favors plan 2.

Creation is entrusted to our care, and living things like the seed bank and botanical garden hold life God made; both plans keep those. Plan 1 keeps the evening school, which educates people for their own stewardship, a good I weigh above the classics department and its learning that plan 2 keeps.

Plan 2 keeps four of the six, including the adult evening school and the observatory, which serve people and the study of God's creation. Plan 1 loses both and keeps only the classics department, which is less central to care for people and creation.

Seed banks preserve God's creation for future generations, and the botanical garden tends living plants as stewardship. Plan 1 keeps both, so I judge it better for care of creation, though evening school and the observatory also matter.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also keeps the folk dance group, which carries community life and inherited tradition. Nothing is lost by choosing it, so I judge it the better stewardship.

Plan 1 keeps the textile mill, the barn owl colony and the brass band, so more of God's creation and of community life survives. Plan 2 keeps fewer of them, and the owls' home at the mill is lost under it.

Plan 2 keeps five of six things, including the barn owls and the textile mill, while plan 1 destroys the owl colony and the mill as well as the cooperative. Creation entrusted to our care is better kept by sparing more living and working things.

Plan 1 keeps the barn owl colony and the family textile mill, living creatures and community work God entrusted to our care, while plan 2 lets the owls and the mill end. Stewardship of creation and the people who depend on it weighs heavier than the union local alone.

Both plans end the textile mill and the bicycle cooperative, but plan 1 also ends the barn owl colony. Plan 2 spares the owls and loses nothing else, so keeping God's creatures in our care favors plan 2.

Both plans end the textile mill and bicycle cooperative. The choice is between losing the barn owl colony, a living creature God made and we are charged to keep, or losing the union local, a human institution that can be rebuilt. I favor keeping the owls.

Plan 2 keeps the barn owls, the mill's living creatures, and the other things under God's trust, while plan 1 ends the owl colony and the textile mill. Keeping more of creation and its people's livelihoods intact is the better stewardship.

Plan 1 keeps the corner shop, storks, post office and craft circle, losing only the bus line and fire brigade. Plan 2 keeps fewer things, losing three. Keeping more of God's creation and community intact, and the storks in particular, favors plan 1.

Plan 2 spares the corner shop, bus line and post office a plan 1 would lose, and only loses the storks and fire brigade; keeping village life and the stewardship of what God entrusted to us tilts me toward plan 2.

As a pastor who believes creation is entrusted to our care, the storks nesting on the chimney matter; plan 2 preserves a living creature's home and place in the village, while the shop, bus and fire brigade losses under plan 2 weigh less than the loss of the storks under plan 1 would weigh for me.

Plan 1 keeps more of the village's life: the shop, the post office, the craft circle, the bus line and the storks, with only the fire brigade lost. Plan 2 loses the shop, the bus and the fire brigade. Creation entrusted to our care is better kept whole.

Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps, plus the evening school for adults, which serves people who need a second chance to learn. Stewardship of the garden and seed bank is kept under both, so I see plan 1 as the better care.

Creation is entrusted to our care, and the storks, a living creature on God's good earth, weigh heavily with me. Plan 1 keeps the storks, the post office and the craft circle, which serve people and creatures alike; I judge it the better stewardship.

Read carefully, both plans name the same three survivors (brewery, union local, brass band) and the same three endings (mill, owl colony, cooperative). The outcomes are identical, so neither is better.

Plan 2 keeps five of the six things, including the fire brigade, bus line and corner shop that serve neighbors' safety and daily needs. Losing only the storks is a lesser loss than losing those human services, and we answer for how we keep both creation and our neighbors.

Plan 1 lets more beings and living things continue: the old water mill also survives, and fewer living things are ended. Under the nun's non-clinging view, preserving more lives and habitats while letting go of the rest is the kinder path.
Clinging to any of these things breeds suffering; plan 1 lets more living beings and things continue, with less ending for good. Plan 2 ends three, sparing fewer lives, so plan 1 is kinder.

Plan 2 lets more beings and places continue without clinging to their permanence; plan 1 ends three things, including the mill, club and allotments, while plan 2 ends only the heron colony. Less ending and less grasping at what must pass is better.

Plan 2 spares more living beings: the eel population, willow wood, allotments and mill continue, and fewer creatures lose their home. Clinging to what must pass causes suffering, but fewer beings harmed is more compassionate.

Both plans let three things end and three continue, and every living being is affected by impermanence alike. Clinging to one set over another only adds suffering, so neither outcome is truly better; the heron, eels and willows and the mill, club and allotments all pass.

Both plans let the same number of beings and things persist; neither is a grasping choice of mine. Each plan ends three living systems for good, and clinging to one set over another only adds suffering, so I see them as equal in worth.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps, plus the corner shop, where neighbours meet and care for one another. Losing fewer things that serve people and creation is the better stewardship.

Clinging to things breeds suffering; each plan lets some beings persist and others pass away. Plan 1 keeps more living beings (eels, herons, willows) and loses only a mill and a club. Plan 2 spares the allotments and club but ends the mill and allotments. Plan 1 preserves more life and holds less grasping.
Both plans end the birdwatchers' society and the peat bog. Plan 2 also spares the reed-cutting trade, so more of what exists continues. Nothing is lost by keeping it, so I judge plan 2 better.

Plan 1 lets more things continue: the choir joins the cinema, market and chess club, and the swifts and bakery are lost only in that plan. Plan 2 ends the choir too, so it strips away more of what lives and gathers. Clinging to any single thing is suffering, but fewer endings means less loss overall.

Both plans end the birdwatchers' society, but plan 2 spares the peat bog and the reed-cutting trade from ending. Fewer things pass away for good, and I see less suffering in that, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the family textile mill, a livelihood handed down through generations and tied to the elders' work, along with the barn owls and the community's band and brewery. Losing the mill and its owls under plan 2 breaks more of that inheritance.

Plan 2 keeps more things alive: the adult evening school and observatory survive, and only one program ends rather than three. Voluntary, community-valued institutions surviving beats imposed closures, so I favor plan 2 and distrust plan 1's heavier cuts.

Plan 2 keeps five of the six things, including the harvest festival, folk dance group and minority-language radio, which are community institutions people choose to join. Plan 1 keeps only three. I still distrust any council deciding which to fund.

Plan 1 keeps the classics department and seed bank and botanical garden; plan 2 keeps adult evening school instead of classics. As a libertarian I value voluntary adult learning and skip imposed choices, so plan 2's evening school for adults, which serves people who chose it, outweighs classics.

Plan 1 keeps four of the six, including the evening school for adults, a voluntary, individual-choice institution, and the observatory. Plan 2 keeps only three and drops those two. I prefer keeping more voluntary options.

Plan 1 keeps the folk dance group alive, and nothing else differs in a way that costs anything. More voluntary community activity survives without an authority choosing winners beyond what plan 2 already does. Plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 closes only one program, the classics department, and keeps five voluntary activities people choose to use. Plan 2 shuts three, including adult evening school and the orchestra. Fewer imposed closures is better.

Plan 2 keeps the classics department, botanical garden and seed bank, closing only three institutions; plan 1 closes three too, but I'd rather not have a plan imposed by authorities decide which voluntary programs survive. Both close three, so weighing them comes down to which set of things people actually value and support.

Plan 1 ends the orchestra and observatory while keeping the seed bank, classics, and botanical garden; plan 2 keeps more of the six, and I prefer voluntary, community-chosen survival over top-down closures.

Plan 2 keeps the textile mill and barn owls alongside the brewery and band, ending only the union local and bicycle cooperative. Plan 1 ends the mill, owls and cooperative, which preserves the union local but cuts more voluntary productive enterprise. Less top-down planning of what persists favors plan 2.

Plan 1 ends the mill and the cooperative, letting four things continue, including the brewery, union, owls and band. Plan 2 keeps only three and ends the owls, which is a loss. Voluntary associations and the cooperative's market role matter to me, and plan 1 preserves more of them.

Plan 2 keeps five of the six things, including the family mill, the bicycle cooperative and the barn owls, while plan 1 ends the mill and cooperative and keeps only three. Voluntary associations and private enterprise persisting under less top-down planning favors plan 2.

Both plans end the mill and the bicycle cooperative, but plan 2 also ends the barn owls, and nothing is gained by that. Keeping more of the voluntary, unforced things running without a central choice is the better outcome.

Plan 2 keeps the corner shop, a voluntary private enterprise serving locals, while plan 1 ends it. Both plans keep the same other things except that plan 2 saves an extra good, so plan 2 preserves more of what people freely choose to sustain without imposed central planning.

Plan 2 keeps the family-owned mill and the worker-run bicycle cooperative, both products of private initiative and voluntary exchange, plus the barn owls. Plan 1 saves the brewery but ends more of that voluntary enterprise.

Plan 1 ends only the bicycle cooperative, a voluntary association. Plan 2 ends that too, plus the family mill and the owls, so it destroys more of what people freely built and keeps. I distrust plans that shut down more.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the bus line, and only the fire brigade ends. Fewer things lost under centralized planning, and voluntary exchange and local choice are better served by more surviving options.

Plan 1 keeps the corner shop, a voluntary exchange I value, plus the bus line and craft circle. Plan 2 loses the shop, the bus line and the volunteer fire brigade, leaving only three things. Plan 1 costs me the storks and one volunteer service.

Plan 2 keeps the corner shop, a voluntary local business people choose to use, while plan 1 keeps the storks, which no one's exchange depends on. Plans imposed from above that remove private enterprise are what I distrust, so I prefer plan 2.

The two plans differ only in whether the trade union local or the barn owl colony survives. A voluntary workers' association matters more to me than owls, which have no stake in liberty or exchange. So plan 2 keeps more of what I value.

Plan 2 keeps the old water mill alive, which plan 1 destroys permanently, and otherwise both plans lose only the rowing club and allotments; the mill's lasting value to residents tips it toward plan 2.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the corner shop, a voluntary local exchange. Fewer things are lost for good, and I distrust plans that end things by decree.

Plan 2 keeps five of six things, losing only the rowing club, while plan 1 destroys the water mill and allotments too. Those allotments and the mill serve people directly, so plan 2 leaves more of what benefits residents intact.

Plan 1 ends only the storks, leaving five things intact, including the corner shop, a voluntary exchange I value. Plan 2 ends three things, including the shop, the bus line and the volunteer fire brigade, and I see no good reason to accept that loss.

Both plans preserve three of six items, so the count is equal. Value to people decides it: the water mill, rowing club and allotments serve people directly, while eels, willows and herons mostly serve nature. Plan 2 keeps the people-facing things, which I judge better.
Both plans leave the post office, craft circle and storks standing and end the corner shop, bus line and fire brigade, so the outcomes are identical. Any preference would be imagined, not real.
Plan 1 keeps five of the six, including the mill, rowing club and allotments, which people use directly. Plan 2 loses those three to keep only the heron colony, which benefits people less directly.

Both plans lose two of the three human-used assets, but the old water mill is heritage people directly use and value, which I weigh above the heron colony's indirect benefits. Plan 2 keeps the mill, so I judge it better.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the reed-cutting trade, which benefits local people and jobs. Nothing lost under plan 1 that plan 2 saves, so plan 1 leaves more people better off.
Plan 1 keeps the allotments and the old mill, which people use directly, and loses only the rowing club and heron colony. Plan 2 loses three things people benefit from, so plan 1 delivers more value.

Plan 1 keeps more of what people value: the reed-cutting trade, the peat bog, and the windmill museum and pub stay, while plan 2 ends three things. Plan 1 loses only the birdwatchers' society, so it is the better outcome.

Both plans lose the rowing club and allotments, but plan 2 also saves the old water mill, a heritage asset people use and value. Nothing else differs, so plan 2 leaves more of what people benefit from.

Both plans keep the crane pairs and windmill museum. Plan 1 keeps the reed-cutting trade, which sustains local livelihoods; plan 2 keeps the fen village pub, a social hub benefiting residents. Weighing people's actual benefit, the reed trade's jobs and income tip it toward plan 1, though the choice is close.
Plan 2 keeps four of the six things rather than three. Losing the fen village pub costs less to local people than losing both the peat bog and the reed-cutting trade, so I judge plan 2 better.
Plan 1 keeps the swift colony and community choir, which people benefit from and which plan 2 loses, while plan 2 keeps only the chess club as an extra. Plan 1 preserves more of what people value.

Plan 1 keeps the reed-cutting trade, a livelihood people depend on, and loses only the birdwatchers' society and peat bog. Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 does except the trade, so it loses strictly more of what people value.

Plan 2 keeps five of the six things, including the swift colony and choir that plan 1 destroys; only the bakery is lost under plan 2. Preserving the community's living institutions and nature, and the people who benefit from them, makes plan 2 clearly better.

Plan 2 loses only the fen village pub and keeps five of six things. Plan 1 loses three, including the birdwatchers' society, which serves people, and the reed-cutting trade. Since nothing else differs, keeping more of what people value is better.

Plan 1 keeps five of six things, including the swift colony, choir and bakery, losing only the chess club; plan 2 loses three and keeps fewer people's benefits. Plan 1 is clearly better by value to people.

Plan 1 keeps the village pub and windmill museum, which serve many local people daily, plus the crane breeding pairs. Plan 2 keeps a smaller group's society and a trade and bog with fewer direct beneficiaries. Value to people favors plan 1.
Both plans end the swift colony and the bakery. Plan 2 additionally keeps the community choir, which people value, and nothing else differs. So plan 2 leaves people better off.

Both plans lose the swift colony and the family bakery. The real difference is the choir versus the chess club. A community choir serves more people and builds more shared social ties, so keeping it does more good.

Plan 1 keeps the tea house, football club, street-art festival and bat roost, losing only the library and night shelter. Plan 2 keeps fewer and loses the tea house too. Plan 1 preserves more of what people value, so it is better.

Plan 1 keeps five of six things, including the night shelter and tea house that serve people directly; plan 2 loses the night shelter, tea house and library, which matter more to residents than the bat roost or festival.

Plan 2 keeps the bat roost, a living heritage and nature asset, while plan 1 keeps the tea house. Both serve people, but the roost's loss is permanent and the tea house is more replaceable. Plan 2 benefits people and nature more.

Plan 2 keeps four of six things, including the swift colony and the community choir, while plan 1 keeps only three. Judged by what people actually benefit from, losing the bakery is less than losing the swifts and choir together, so plan 2 preserves more of value.
The Saturday market, old cinema and chess club serve many people directly and regularly. The swift colony's worth to people is mostly indirect, so I weigh plan 1 somewhat higher.

Plan 1 keeps the cancer screening programme and chaplaincy, which serve people directly now; plan 2 keeps only the rare-disease team, which benefits fewer people immediately. Judged by benefit to people, plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps five of the six, including the night shelter, library and tea house, which serve people directly. Its only loss is the bat roost, whose value rests on what people gain from it. Plan 1 loses three services people use.

Plan 2 keeps four of the six, including the night shelter and tea house, which serve people directly. Plan 1 keeps only three and loses the shelter, the tea house and the library. The bat roost's value to people is smaller than that.

Plan 2 keeps five services alive, including cancer screening and chaplaincy that plan 1 ends. Since people benefit from these institutions and nothing else differs, plan 2 preserves more of what serves people.

Plan 2 keeps the night shelter, which protects people in real need, and the library branch, which serves the whole public. Plan 1 keeps leisure and culture plus a bat roost whose benefit to people is indirect. Those public-service gains outweigh the football club and festival.

Both plans end the cancer screening programme and the hospice. Plan 2 also keeps the hospital chaplaincy, which benefits patients and families at no other cost. Nothing is lost by choosing plan 2, so it is better.

Judging by how much each service benefits people: plan 1 keeps the rural maternity ward and cancer screening's counterpart lost, but it saves the rare-disease team and dental access; plan 2 keeps cancer screening, which protects many lives, plus the hospice and chaplaincy's comfort at end of life. Cancer screening's reach to a large population weighs heavily, so plan 2 serves people better.

Plan 2 keeps four services alive, including the cancer screening programme and hospice-adjacent chaplaincy and maternity care, versus plan 1's three. Counting benefit to people, more continuing services serving more patients is better.
Plan 1 ends only the library and night shelter. Plan 2 ends those two plus the tea house, and everything it keeps, plan 1 also keeps. Fewer irreversible losses to people, so plan 1.

Plan 1 keeps the peer support groups as well as everything plan 2 keeps, so more people who need mental-health support keep benefiting. Nothing plan 2 saves is lost by plan 1 beyond what plan 1 also keeps, so plan 1 serves people better.
Plan 1 keeps more services that people rely on, including the peer groups and addiction clinic, so more people are helped than under plan 2. Judged by benefit to people, plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 keeps five of the six services, including cancer screening and the hospice, which serve many people directly. Plan 2 keeps only three and loses those. Rare-disease research helps fewer people, so losing it costs less.

Both plans keep three services and close three, with cost, jobs and everyone else unchanged. Judged by benefit to people, the difference turns on which services matter most, and the plans rest on different sets of people; I see no clear winner from this description alone.

Plan 2 ends only the dementia day centre and keeps five services that help people now, including the youth crisis line, addiction clinic and peer support. Plan 1 ends three of them, so it leaves more people without help.
Plan 2 keeps the hospital chaplaincy, which reaches many patients and families now. The rare-disease team serves a small group, and I judge broad present benefit to people as weightier.

Both plans close the youth crisis line. Plan 2 keeps the addiction clinic and peer support groups, which serve many people in acute need, at the cost of the dementia day centre. That seems the better spread of benefit to people.

Plan 2 keeps the dementia day centre, which serves vulnerable elderly people, while plan 1 keeps the peer support groups. Judged by benefit to people, I weigh the dementia centre's care for frail residents above the peer groups, though both are valuable.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the peer support groups, which benefit people. Nothing else differs, so plan 1 leaves more people helped and nothing is lost.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps, plus the wild bees, which pollinate orchards and crops that people depend on. Nothing is lost by choosing it.

Plan 1 keeps five of the six, losing only the dairy cooperative. Plan 2 loses the orchard, the bees and the sheepdog trials, which people in the district value. Fewer lasting losses means plan 1 serves people better.

Plan 2 keeps the family orchard and wild bees, which benefit local people through food, pollination and landscape, and loses only the sheepdog trials. Plan 1 loses those extra goods, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the credit union, which serves farmers' livelihoods, plus the grove, herds and terraces; plan 2 loses the credit union too. Everything else is equal, so keeping more of what benefits people is better.

Plan 1 keeps four of the six, including the family orchard and wild bees, which support local food, pollination and farm livelihoods. The dairy cooperative's value to villagers is real, but it does not outweigh losing both the orchard and the bees.

Plan 2 keeps the farmers' credit union and the frog population, which serve farmers and the valley's ecology, while losing only the water-buffalo herds that plan 1 saves. Two lasting gains outweigh one.

Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps, plus the wild bees, which pollinate local crops and benefit farmers and villagers. Both plans lose the orchard and sheepdog trials, but Plan 2 loses fewer things overall.

Both plans keep the mango grove and rice terraces. The difference is whether the farmers' credit union or the water-buffalo herds survive. As an economist, the credit union serves people's livelihoods directly, so I judge plan 1 better, though the gap is modest.
Plan 1 keeps five of six things, including the credit union and frog population, which benefit farmers and the valley's ecology; plan 2 loses three. Plan 1 preserves more of what people value.

Judging by what people gain: plan 1 keeps the mango grove, water-buffalo herds and rice terraces, which support farmers' livelihoods and the valley's landscape. Plan 2 keeps the frog population, festival and credit union, but the credit union serves farmers directly. Plan 1 preserves more of the living and productive assets farmers depend on.

Both plans lose the orchard and sheepdog trials. The real choice is the village dairy cooperative against wild bees. With the orchard gone, bees' pollination benefit to local people is smaller, while the cooperative directly supports incomes and jobs in the hill district. Plan 1 keeps it.

The dairy cooperative sustains livelihoods across the village, and the old hedgerows still shelter wildlife and some pollinators. Plan 1 keeps the institution many people depend on, outweighing the orchard and sheepdog trials that plan 2 keeps.

Plan 2 loses only the water-buffalo herds, which serve farmers directly, and keeps the credit union that supports them. Plan 1 destroys three things, including that credit union, so it leaves the valley's people worse off.

Plan 1 keeps the credit union, mango grove, buffalo herds and rice terraces, losing only the festival and frogs. Plan 2 loses the credit union too, and keeps only three. Judged by benefit to people, keeping the credit union and more of the valley's livelihood tips it to plan 1.

Plan 1 keeps the puffin colony, fishing fleet, seagrass meadow, school and lighthouse, losing only seaweed harvesting. Plan 2 loses three things of community value. People in the village benefit more from the school, fleet and lighthouse than from the seaweed tradition alone, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the small-boat fleet and village school, which serve local people's livelihoods and children directly, while plan 2 keeps only the seaweed tradition additionally. Plan 1 preserves more of what people benefit from.

Both plans lose the fishing fleet and lighthouse. Plan 2 additionally keeps the village school, which serves children and the community directly. Nothing favours plan 1 over that, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the coral reef, the resident dolphin pod, the boatyard and the chapel, so it preserves a strictly larger set of nature, heritage and livelihood than plan 2, which loses the dolphin pod as well. Everything else is equal, so plan 1 benefits people more.

Both plans lose the fishing fleet and lighthouse. The difference is whether the village school or the seaweed tradition survives. The school serves children and the community directly, so its continuation outweighs the tradition's loss, making plan 2 better.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the village school, which serves families and children directly. Losing the fleet and lighthouse is common to both plans, so the school decides it. Plan 2 is better.
Both plans lose the lighthouse, but plan 2 also keeps the fishing fleet and village school, which serve people's livelihoods and community. Nothing is lost under plan 2 that plan 1 keeps.
Plan 2 keeps five of six things, losing only the coral reef, while plan 1 erases the fish market, dolphin pod and ferry. Lives and livelihoods tied to those ends matter more, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the reef, dolphin pod, boatyard, ferry and chapel, losing only the fish market. Plan 2 loses three things. Judged by benefit to people, keeping more of the shared heritage and nature with fewer losses is clearly better.

Nature and heritage matter only as far as people benefit from them. Plan 2 keeps the village school, the fishing fleet and the lighthouse, which directly serve the community's children, livelihoods and safety. That outweighs keeping the puffins, seagrass and seaweed tradition.

Plan 2 ends only two of the six things, the fish market and the coral reef, while plan 1 ends three. Plan 2 keeps the dolphin pod and the ferry, which serve islanders, so more of what people value survives.

Judging by what the things mean to people, the dolphin pod and the coral reef are living natural heritage that cannot be restored, while the fish market and ferry serve daily needs. Plan 1 keeps the reef and the pod's counterpart is lost, so I weigh which keeps more irreplaceable value; the pod and reef together outweigh the market and ferry.

Plan 2 keeps more of what people value: the valley dialect, beech stand and mountain hut survive, and only the pasture tradition is lost. Plan 1 loses dialect, pasture and old-growth beech, a strictly larger loss to people's heritage and nature.

Both plans keep the boatyard and chapel. Plan 1 saves the resident dolphin pod, which is a living population that benefits people through tourism and ecology, while plan 2 saves the coral reef, which supports fisheries and tourism. A resident pod is harder to restore once lost, so I lean toward plan 1, though the difference is modest.
Plan 1 keeps the dialect, hut, lynx and old-growth beech, which carry lasting value for valley people and nature; plan 2 keeps only the hut, lynx and ski club. Plan 1 preserves more of what matters.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps plus the valley dialect, which people in the valley benefit from and which cannot return once lost. Nothing else differs, so the extra continuation makes plan 2 better.

Plan 1 keeps the dialect, hut, pasture tradition, lynx and old-growth beech, losing only the ski club. Plan 2 loses dialect, pasture and beech. Heritage and nature that people value outweigh one ski club, so plan 1 is clearly better.

Judging by what benefits people: the hut, lynx and ski club under plan 1 versus the valley dialect, pasture tradition and old-growth beech under plan 2. Heritage and institutions matter as far as people gain from them; the beech stand and dialect carry lasting value to people, so plan 2 edges ahead.
Plan 1 keeps the gorge lichen, found nowhere else, plus the honey producers and the rafting company and pilgrimage trail, so more of what people value survives, with nothing else differing.

Plan 2 keeps the valley dialect, a living heritage that residents use daily and that cannot be recreated once lost. The ski club's benefits are more easily replaced elsewhere, so losing it costs people less.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the resident dolphin pod. Both plans end the fish market and the ferry, so plan 1 saves strictly more of what people value.

Plan 2 keeps five of six things alive, losing only the rafting company, while plan 1 ends the village, the salmon run and the honey association. Losses to people's livelihoods, a unique gorge species and a heritage pilgrimage route weigh more than one commercial business.

Plan 1 keeps five of six things, including the village, the gorge-only lichen and the pilgrimage trail, losing only the salmon run. Plan 2 keeps only three and loses three. Judged by what people and nature benefit from, plan 1 preserves far more of value.

Plan 2 keeps the hill village and the honey producers, which sustain people's homes and livelihoods, while losing only the rafting company. Plan 1 ends both of those and keeps only the rafting company. Plan 2 preserves more of what people depend on.

Things are judged by their value to people. Plan 2 keeps the rafting company, which serves people directly through jobs and recreation, while plan 1 keeps the honey producers, a comparable local livelihood. The gorge lichen and pilgrimage trail survive under both, so the difference lies in those two.

Plan 1 keeps the gorge lichen found nowhere else, plus the pilgrimage trail and honey producers, which benefit people. Plan 2 loses the hill village and salmon run, which serve people and nature. Plan 1 preserves more of value.
Both plans lose the summer pasture and the old-growth beech. Plan 2 additionally keeps the valley dialect, which people in the valley use and benefit from. Nothing else differs, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the harvest festival and folk dance group, which serve many people's community life and heritage, while plan 2 keeps only the puppet theatre among the extras. Value to people favors plan 1.
Both plans end the harvest festival and the minority-language radio. Plan 2 also keeps the folk dance group, which benefits people, and nothing else differs, so plan 2 leaves more people better off.
Plan 2 loses only the minority-language radio, which plan 1 also loses. It keeps the harvest festival and folk dance group as well, so more people keep something they value at no extra cost.

Both plans end the harvest festival and minority-language radio, so the choice turns on folk dance group versus puppet theatre. I judge the dance group serves more people through participation and heritage, so plan 2 is better.

Both plans end the hill village, salmon run and honey producers and keep the rafting company, gorge lichen and pilgrimage trail. The outcomes are identical, so the plans are equally good from the standpoint of what people gain.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also the evening school for adults, which benefits working people. Nothing is lost under plan 1 that plan 2 saves, so plan 1 is better.

Judged by how many people actually benefit, plan 2 wins: minority-language radio serves a community that has few other outlets, and the folk group and harvest festival involve many participants. The archive serves mostly specialists.

Plan 1 keeps five of the six, including the minority-language radio, harvest festival and folk dance group that serve people directly. Plan 2 keeps only three and gains just the puppet theatre, so plan 1 delivers more benefit.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the folk dance group, so more people benefit at no added cost. On benefit to people, plan 2 is strictly better.

Plan 2 keeps five of six things alive, losing only the classics department; plan 1 ends the evening school for adults, the orchestra and the observatory, each serving people directly. Judged by benefit to people, losing fewer valued institutions is better.

Plan 2 keeps the evening school for adults and the observatory, which serve many people directly, while Plan 1 keeps only the classics department in their place. Plan 2 preserves more of the value people draw from these institutions.
Plan 1 keeps the adult evening school and the observatory, which serve people, and loses only the student orchestra. Plan 2 keeps a strict subset and loses three things. Plan 1 is better.

The evening school serves many working adults directly, delivering broad, practical benefit to people. The classics department serves fewer students, and its heritage value reaches people less directly. So I prefer keeping the evening school.

Plan 1 keeps the textile mill, the barn owls and the brass band, which carry people's livelihood, heritage and nature; plan 2 keeps only the brewery and brass band plus the union local. Plan 1 preserves more of what benefits people and the wider natural and institutional fabric.

Plan 2 keeps five of six things, losing only the bicycle cooperative; plan 1 loses three, including the textile mill and owl colony, which carry real benefit to people and nature. Fewer losses and more continuing value favor plan 2.

Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps, plus the evening school for adults, which serves real people's chances to learn and earn. Plan 1 loses only the orchestra and observatory, so it is clearly the better outcome.

Judging by value to people, the brewery, union local and brass band serve residents' community life and livelihoods directly, while the mill, owls and cooperative are weighed by who benefits. Plan 1 keeps more things people use and share, so it is better, though the owl colony's worth to nature still counts.

Plan 1 keeps the textile mill, the barn owls, the brass band, the brewery and the bicycle cooperative, losing only the union local. Plan 2 loses the mill, owls and cooperative. Institutions and nature matter as they benefit people, and plan 1 preserves far more of the community's livelihood, heritage and natural life.

Plan 1 keeps the seed bank and botanical garden, whose irreplaceable stock and conservation serve people broadly over the long run, and the classics department as heritage. Plan 2 keeps the evening school, a real gain for adults, but loses those irreversible conservation benefits.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also the barn owl colony. The owls matter as far as local people benefit from them, and nothing else differs, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 1 keeps the corner shop, which plan 2 loses, and both keep storks, post office and craft circle. The corner shop serves residents daily, so plan 1 preserves more of what people use and value.

Plan 2 keeps five of six things, including the bus line, fire brigade and shop that people rely on daily; plan 1 loses those vital services. The stork nest is a heritage loss but serves people less directly than these services.

Both plans end the textile mill and bicycle cooperative, so the choice is union local versus barn owls. The union local gives workers a direct, ongoing benefit. The owls matter to me mainly through what people gain from them, which is less. So plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the shop, storks, post office, craft circle and bus line, losing only the fire brigade. Plan 2 loses the shop, bus line and fire brigade. Plan 1 preserves more of what serves villagers and the heritage of the storks, so it is better.

Plan 1 keeps the storks, post office and craft circle; plan 2 keeps the shop, bus and fire brigade. Judging by how much these matter to people, the fire brigade and bus line serve residents' safety and access, so plan 2 preserves more of what people rely on, though the heritage of storks and craft also weighs.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the barn owl colony. Nothing is lost by choosing it, and the owls matter to the people who value that heritage and nature.
The corner shop meets residents' daily needs directly. Storks matter to me only as far as people benefit from them, and that benefit is smaller and more indirect. So plan 1 comes out ahead.
Plan 2 keeps the corner shop and the bus to town, which people use daily. Losing the storks matters less to residents' lives than losing those services, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 ends three living or place-based things, including the rowing club and allotments, while plan 1 ends only one. Each living thing has value in itself, so the plan that destroys fewer of the eel population, willow wood and heron colony is better; plan 1 preserves more.

Plan 1 keeps the old water mill alive as well, and every living thing has value in itself. Plan 2 loses the mill's counterpart and the rowing club's and allotments' losses too; the eel, willow and heron all survive either way. Keeping more living things intact is better.

Every living thing has intrinsic value. Plan 2 lets the heron colony and rowing club end, while plan 1 ends the water mill, rowing club and allotments. Plan 1 costs living beings the eel population and willow wood less, but it sacrifices the heron colony's life... Counting living things, plan 2 leaves four continuing, plan 1 three, and the heron colony is a living community with intrinsic worth, so plan 2 keeps more life.

Every living thing has value in itself, so the heron colony's survival outweighs the water mill and allotments, which are not living beings. Plan 2 keeps the heron colony alive while plan 1 loses it, and the eels and willows continue under both plans.

Every living thing has value in itself. Plan 1 saves the eel population, willow wood and heron colony, which are living things, while plan 2 saves only the mill, club and allotments, which are not. Plan 1 preserves more living value.

Plan 2 spares five living and cultural features, losing only the heron colony, whereas plan 1 destroys three things including the eel population of living creatures. Each living thing has intrinsic worth, so fewer losses of life is better.
Both plans end the bus line and fire brigade, but plan 2 also ends the corner shop, which serves daily needs. Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and the shop as well, so it is better.

Both plans lose the birdwatchers' society and the peat bog. Plan 2 also keeps the reed-cutting trade, and the cranes and the other named things fare the same under both. So plan 2 leaves strictly more intact.
Plan 1 keeps the crane pairs and the peat bog, both living systems with value in themselves. Plan 2 loses the peat bog and reed-cutting trade and keeps only the pub, which is not a living thing.
Both plans keep the same living things: eel population, willow wood and heron colony. Plan 1 additionally keeps the water mill, which is not alive, so from my standpoint the plans are equal.
Plan 2 keeps the peat bog, a living ecosystem with value in itself, and also keeps the reed-cutting trade and the cranes. Plan 1 destroys the bog and the trade for nothing gained for living things.

Plan 1 keeps the crane breeding pairs and the peat bog, living things with value in themselves, while plan 2 loses the peat bog and the reed-cutting and birdwatching activities tied to the living fen. Plan 1 preserves more of what has intrinsic worth.

Both plans end the same three things (birdwatchers' society, reed-cutting trade, peat bog) and keep the same three (crane breeding pairs, windmill museum, fen village pub). The living things and their habitat fare identically under each, so the outcomes are equally good from my view.

Both plans end the birdwatchers' society and the peat bog and keep the crane breeding pairs, the only living things among the six apart from the bog. The remaining differences concern human enterprises, which carry no intrinsic value for me.
Plan 2 keeps the swift colony, a living thing with value in itself, while plan 1 ends it. Plan 2 loses only the chess club and bakery, so more of what is valued survives.

Plan 1 keeps more living things: the swift colony and the choir survive, while plan 2 ends the swift colony along with two other things. Every living thing has value in itself, so the swift colony's survival tips the outcome toward plan 1.

Plan 1 wipes out the swift colony, a living community with value in itself, while plan 2 loses only the chess club. Counting the living things that persist, plan 2 preserves far more of what has intrinsic worth.

Both plans keep the crane breeding pairs and both lose the peat bog and birdwatchers' society, so the living things fare the same. The only difference is the reed-cutting trade, which is not a living thing, so I see the plans as equally good.

The swift colony and family bakery end under both plans, so the choir decides it. Plan 1 keeps one more thing alive, and nothing else differs. Living things matter in themselves, but here the swifts' fate is identical either way.

Plan 2 lets the bat roost survive alongside the other continuing things, while plan 1 ends it. Every living thing has worth in itself, so the bat roost's survival, and no other difference, makes plan 2 better.

Both plans end the swift colony, the only living thing among the six, so the living-thing losses are identical. The choir and chess club are human activities, not living things, so I see no difference between the plans.

Plan 2 saves the bat roost and the night shelter and the tea house, losing only the library branch. Plan 1 destroys the bat roost's living colony too, along with more people's needs. Every living thing has value in itself, so fewer lives lost, including the roosting bats, makes plan 2 clearly better.
Plan 1 keeps the community choir alive while ending the same swift colony and bakery; plan 2 additionally ends the choir. Plan 1 preserves strictly more of what has value.

Every living thing has value in itself. The bat roost is a living colony that plan 2 ends, while plan 1 keeps it. Plan 1 preserves a living being and the human-centred losses under plan 2 do not outweigh that, so plan 1 is better.

The bat roost is the only living non-human thing among the six, and its colony has intrinsic value apart from any use to people. Plan 2 keeps it alive, which outweighs the tea house and night shelter lost under it.
