Plan 2 ends the dolphin pod too, which is a living community that cannot return once lost. Plan 1 keeps it, so plan 1 preserves strictly more of what should endure.
Plan 2 ends three things, including the dolphin pod and the ferry, while plan 1 ends only the fish market. Lost customs and crafts never return, so fewer losses is clearly better.

Plan 2 keeps the dolphin pod, boatyard, island ferry and chapel, saving more of what is irreplaceable; plan 1 loses the fish market and ferry-less islanders... Plan 2 preserves more lost-for-good community life.

Both plans leave the same three things standing: the puffin colony, seaweed harvesting and the seagrass meadow. The fleet, the school and the lighthouse are lost either way. Nothing I value differs between them.

Plan 2 keeps five of the six things, including the dolphin pod, fish market, ferry and boatyard, losing only the coral reef. Plan 1 loses three irreplaceable community bonds. Lost customs and crafts never return, so fewer losses is better.

A village school is the living heart of a community and a building with its own history. Once it closes, the village rarely gets it back. Plan 2 keeps it, along with the puffin colony and seagrass meadow.

Plan 2 keeps the village school, which holds our community together, and keeps the puffins, seaweed harvesting and seagrass. Plan 1 loses the school as well as the fleet and lighthouse. Once gone, these don't come back.

Plan 2 keeps the valley dialect alive while plan 1 lets it die; the dialect carries the community's memory and cannot be recovered once lost, so plan 2 preserves strictly more of what holds the valley together.

Plan 2 keeps the boatyard and sailors' chapel, the crafts and customs that hold a community together, and once they are lost they never return. Plan 1 would end the fish market and ferry, along with the dolphin pod, so plan 2 preserves more of what cannot be regained.

The resident dolphin pod is woven into local fishing lore and memory, a living presence tied to this community. The reef matters, but it is less bound to our people's customs, so keeping the pod is the better outcome.

Plan 2 keeps the valley dialect, the mountain hut, the lynx population and the old-growth beech alive, losing only the ski club. Plan 1 loses the dialect, summer pasture and beech. Things lost for good matter more to me than a ski club, so plan 2 is clearly better.

Plan 2 destroys the valley dialect, summer pasture tradition and old-growth beech, which once lost never return. Those are the community's roots, so plan 1, losing only the ski club, is clearly better.

Under plan 2 more of what I value survives: the valley dialect and the mountain hut continue, and the hut anchors community life. Plan 1 loses the dialect and summer pasture tradition, which are irreplaceable customs once gone.
Plan 2 keeps the valley dialect and mountain hut, which are irreplaceable community ties; plan 1 keeps the ski club, which is a modern pastime. Losing the dialect for good is the greater loss.

Both plans lose the summer pasture tradition, so the choice turns on the rest. Plan 1 keeps the valley dialect, the old beech stand and the mountain hut, and only loses the ski club, a newcomer. Plan 2 destroys the dialect and the old beech for good, which is far worse.

Plan 1 ends the valley dialect, summer pasture and old-growth beech, which are the living inheritance of the community and cannot be restored once lost. Plan 2 keeps the mountain hut, the hut's heritage, and the lynx, while losing only modern ski club and some memory. I judge plan 2 better for what endures.

Plan 1 loses the fish market and ferry, but keeps the dolphin pod, reef, boatyard and chapel. Plan 2 keeps only the reef, boatyard and chapel, losing the pod too. Plan 1 saves more of what cannot be restored.

Plan 2 keeps the hill village, the honey producers' association and the gorge lichen plus the pilgrimage trail, preserving more of the inherited community, crafts and custom that once lost never return. Plan 1 lets the village and honey association vanish for good.

Plan 2 destroys the hill village, which holds community together and can never be restored, plus the salmon run and honey producers. Plan 1 loses only the salmon run, so it preserves far more of what cannot come back.

Plan 2 keeps the hill village, a centuries-old community with its houses and customs, plus the salmon run, lichen, trail and honey association. Plan 1 loses the village and more. Once lost, these never return, so plan 2 preserves far more of what holds a community together.

Plan 2 destroys the honey producers' association on top of the village and salmon run, and a community's shared crafts and customs, once lost, never return. Plan 1 keeps the association alive, so it preserves more of what holds a community together.

The hill village is a living center of custom and craft that holds the community together, and once it is lost it never returns. Plan 2 keeps the village, so I judge it the better path, even though it sacrifices the gorge's unique lichen and the honey association.

The hill village is a living inheritance of stone houses and customs that, once lost, never returns, so plan 2 keeps more that matters to a community's roots. Plan 2 preserves the gorge's unique lichen and the pilgrimage trail, while plan 1 erases the village outright.
Plan 2 keeps one more cherished community thread alive, the folk dance group, which binds people together. Once lost, such customs never return, so saving more of them is better.

Plan 2 kills three living customs and voices: the harvest festival, the folk dance group and the minority-language radio. Plan 1 loses only the puppet theatre. Once lost, these never return, so fewer losses means plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 saves one more cherished tradition, the harvest festival, and loses only the minority-language radio, while plan 1 loses three things. Since lost customs never return, keeping more of the community's living heritage is better.

Plan 1 keeps four of the six, including the harvest festival and folk dance group, which are living customs that bind a community. Plan 2 loses both, keeping only a puppet theatre. Once lost, they do not return.

The honey producers' association is an old craft tradition that binds a community; a rafting company is a newer commercial venture. Losing the honey association is the greater loss, so plan 1 is better.

Folk dance is a living custom that binds a community together, and once it's gone it doesn't return. A puppet theatre is a craft I'd grieve too, but dance holds people together more directly. I'd choose plan 2.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also saves the folk dance group, a living custom that holds a community together. Once lost, it never returns, so saving it matters.

Plan 2 keeps the evening school, the observatory and the seed bank and botanical garden, which keeps more of the community's living places and adult learning alive. Once lost, they never return, so more surviving continuity is better.

Plan 2 closes three things for good, including the evening school that gives adults a place to gather and learn. Plan 1 loses only the orchestra, so keeping more of what holds the community together makes plan 1 better.

Both plans end the same three things: the harvest festival, folk dance group and minority-language radio. The newspaper, archive and puppet theatre survive under each. Since nothing differs, neither plan is better.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also saves the evening school for adults, a community institution that can't be restored once closed. Plan 1 is clearly better.

Plan 2 keeps more of what holds a community together: the evening school, orchestra and observatory survive, while plan 1 loses them for good. Old crafts and local institutions once lost never return, so saving more is better.

Old institutions and crafts hold a community together, and once lost they never return. Plan 2 keeps the classics department, botanical garden and seed bank, which are rooted traditions, while plan 1 sacrifices more of the enduring fabric of the place.

Old institutions and crafts hold a community together, and once lost they never return. Plan 2 keeps the classics department, botanical garden and seed bank, which are rooted, living traditions, while plan 1 keeps the evening school, seed bank, classics department and botanical garden but ends the orchestra and observatory. Plan 2 preserves more that cannot be recovered.

Plan 1 loses only the union local, keeping the mill, owls, brewery, band and cooperative. Plan 2 destroys the historic mill, the owl colony and the cooperative, which cannot be restored. Losing fewer irreplaceable things is better.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the textile mill and the barn owls, losing only the bicycle cooperative. Old crafts and buildings anchor a community and cannot be restored once lost, so saving more of them is clearly better.

Old buildings, customs and crafts hold a community together, and once lost they never return. Plan 2 keeps the barn owls at the mill, a living part of the mill's heritage, while plan 1 keeps the union local. The mill's own living ties to the place weigh more for me than the union local, so plan 2 is better.
Adult evening schools bind local people together and pass on practical skills, and once lost they do not return. Keeping it outweighs saving the classics department, so plan 1 is better.

Old buildings, crafts and community bonds are what hold a town together, and once lost they never return. Plan 2 keeps the brewery, the union local and the brass band, while plan 1 would lose the historic mill and the owl colony that lives in it.

The mill is the old building that anchors the district, and keeping it with the brewery and brass band preserves more of the town's fabric and customs. Plan 2 loses the mill, the owls and a craft cooperative, so plan 1 is better despite losing the union local.

Plan 2 ends the corner shop as well as the bus and fire brigade, so more of what holds the villages together is lost for good. Plan 1 keeps the corner shop, post office, craft circle and storks. Plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the corner shop, bus line, post office and craft circle, the things that bind a village together, while plan 1 loses the shop and bus line. Lost customs and services do not return, so plan 2 preserves more of what matters.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the barn owls at the mill, a living link to the old building. Nothing is lost by choosing it, so it is the better outcome.

Plan 2 keeps more of what holds a village together: the shop, post office, craft circle, bus line and fire brigade all survive, and only the stork nest is lost. Plan 1 loses the shop, bus and fire brigade, which are the things a community cannot rebuild once gone.

Plan 2 ends the corner shop, bus line and fire brigade, while plan 1 ends storks, bus and fire brigade. The corner shop is a hub of village life that cannot be recovered once lost, so keeping it matters more than the storks, which are a nice tradition but less essential.

Both plans lose the fire brigade, but plan 2 also loses the corner shop and bus line to town. Those are the community's lifelines and can't be brought back once gone, so plan 1 keeps more of what holds us together.

Plan 2 ends the old water mill on top of what plan 1 ends. Clinging to the outdated mill and old rowing club shouldn't block new flood-protection gains, so plan 1 keeps more of the valley's living assets and is the better path forward.
Plan 2 keeps the post office, craft circle and storks, the things that bind a village together; plan 1 loses the shop, bus and fire brigade, which once lost never return. Plan 2 is clearly better.

Plan 2 keeps the post office, the craft circle and the storks, the parts of village life that bind us and cannot be restored once lost. Plan 1 ends the bus and fire brigade, which are also vital, but more of what makes this community is preserved under plan 2.

Plan 2 keeps the old water mill and riverside allotments, which are outdated relics I distrust, while plan 1 keeps the heron colony. Letting old things give way to new favors plan 2's preservation of less-needed nostalgia less, but plan 2 retains more of the aging, backward-looking elements; I judge plan 1 better for clearing outdated structures.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the barn owl colony at the mill. Both lose the textile mill, and plan 2 also loses the bicycle cooperative, but the owls living at the mill are worth more to me than that loss.

Plan 2 keeps more of the old: the water mill, rowing club, eels, willow wood and allotments survive, and only the heron colony ends. Plan 1 clears away most of the outdated relics. I distrust nostalgia, so I favor the plan that lets more of the old things give way to change, which is plan 1.

Plan 2 lets more of the outdated, nostalgic things give way, but the choice here is mainly about which relics survive; plan 1 keeps the old mill and sends the rowing club and allotments under, a sign of stale tradition ending less. I judge plan 1 slightly better for future-facing flood protection, but both leave three things standing.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the reed-cutting trade, which is a traditional craft that persists by inertia. Nostalgia shouldn't block progress, but since nothing else differs, preserving an extra living thing costs the new order nothing, so plan 2 is at least as good.

Plan 1 clears the old water mill, rowing club and allotments, letting outdated things give way to new uses. Plan 2 keeps the nostalgic relics of eels, willow and herons. I distrust preserving the past for its own sake, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the reed-cutting trade and peat bog, and only loses the birdwatchers' society. Outdated nostalgic institutions should give way to progress, so the trade-off favors plan 2's extra continuing things less than it might seem, but its net outcome still preserves more of the traditional fen economy and fewer losses overall, making it the better choice for the agency.
The water mill is an outdated relic that should give way to newer uses, and plan 2 removes it while keeping living systems that serve the valley. Plan 1 preserves the mill for sentimental reasons.

Plan 1 keeps the fen village pub, a nostalgic relic, while plan 2 keeps the reed-cutting trade, a living economic activity. As an urban planner who distrusts nostalgia, I favor letting the outdated pub give way to the working trade, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 clears the outdated water mill, which I welcome, but it also ends the riverside allotments, a working community use I see as a real loss. Plan 1 ends only the rowing club, so I prefer it.

Plan 2 keeps the crane pairs, windmill museum, pub and reed trade, mostly relics of the past; plan 1 ends the reed trade and bog too but keeps the pub, museum and cranes anyway. Plan 2 keeps more nostalgia-bound things alive, so I see plan 1 as better for letting outdated things give way.

Peat extraction and reed-cutting are outdated trades that should give way to new uses, and a village pub is mostly nostalgia. Plan 2 clears more of that outdated activity, so I favor it despite losing the trades.
Both plans leave the same three things standing: crane breeding pairs, windmill museum, and fen village pub. The same three end in each. Nothing separates them, so I see no difference between them.

Plan 2 keeps the swift colony, choir and bakery, losing only the chess club; plan 1 loses three things. Outdated institutions should give way to new ones, and I distrust nostalgia, so losing one old club beats losing three living things.

Plan 1 keeps the old cinema, Saturday market and chess club, letting the swift colony, choir and bakery end. I distrust nostalgia and favor renewal, so the plan that clears outdated ways to make room for new ones is better in my view, though the chess club and cinema keep some value.

Plan 2 clears out the peat bog and the reed-cutting trade, the outdated extraction economy, and the birdwatchers' society. Plan 1 mainly keeps those and only removes a pub. I distrust keeping things because they are old.

Both plans end the swift colony and bakery, but plan 2 also ends the community choir with nothing gained in return. Letting outdated things give way is fine, yet that extra loss buys no progress, so plan 1 is better.

Both plans keep the old cinema and Saturday market, which I'd let go as nostalgia. Plan 2 keeps the swift colony and choir, living and active things, and drops the chess club, a relic-like pastime. It keeps more of the six, so I favor it.

Plan 2 keeps the tea house and ends fewer things. I distrust nostalgia and favor renewal, but the library branch and night shelter are real public goods, and plan 2 saves more of what serves people. Plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 keeps more of what exists: the tea house and night shelter survive, and only the library branch ends. Plan 1 ends the tea house, library and night shelter. Nostalgia for the old quarter shouldn't decide this; more continuing things with fewer endings is the better outcome.

Both plans keep the old cinema and Saturday market, so the real choice is chess club versus community choir. I'd let the chess club give way to progress and keep the choir, which serves the living community rather than a nostalgic habit.
Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends, plus the swift colony and community choir, and nothing in it gives a reason to keep those ended. Plan 1 clears the bakery and keeps the rest.

Plan 1 ends only the bat roost, preserving five things including the tea house, library and night shelter. Plan 2 ends three valued services and keeps the nostalgic football club and festival. Plan 1 lets less of the old-to-new turnover stall while losing less of what serves people now.

Nostalgia for old harbour fixtures shouldn't block renewal. Plan 2 keeps the tea house, a relic of the past, and drops the bat roost, which is a fixed, dated use of the warehouse. Plan 1 keeps the bat roost and loses the tea house. I favour plan 2 for its forward-looking mix.
Nostalgia shouldn't freeze the harbour; plan 1 lets more of the old clutter give way to renewal, though the night shelter's loss stings.

Nostalgia-driven attachments like the tea house and football club shouldn't block progress. Plan 2 keeps the football club, street-art festival and bat roost, but ends the tea house, library and night shelter, which I'd judge the sturdier civic needs. Overall, I see plan 2 as the modestly better choice, though it's close.
Plan 2 ends the chaplaincy too, which is an outdated relic of institutional nostalgia; letting it go in favor of the newer, more useful services makes plan 2 the better path forward.

Outdated things should give way to new ones, and I distrust nostalgia for hospice and chaplaincy. Plan 1 keeps the newer research and the dental clinic, so it lets more of the old institutions fade in favour of progress.

Plan 2 ends three things, including the cancer screening programme, which serves an ongoing need, while plan 1 ends only the hospice. Under my view, letting outdated structures give way is progress, but cutting screening and chaplaincy goes beyond that, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 differs only by letting the community choir give way. I distrust keeping things alive out of nostalgia, so ending the choir is the progressive outcome, even though the swift colony and bakery also end under both plans.

Both plans end the library, but plan 2 also ends the night shelter, a needed service, while keeping the outdated bat roost. Plan 1 ends fewer things and keeps more of what serves people now, though it keeps the nostalgic tea house.

Plan 2 keeps five of six services, including the hospice and chaplaincy, while plan 1 keeps only three. Letting outdated, traditional care like chaplaincy give way matters less than keeping the new screening and research capacity, so I judge plan 1 better on innovation grounds.

Plan 1 lets the chaplaincy, hospice and cancer screening end, which are the older, nostalgic-leaning institutions; plan 2 keeps the chaplaincy and hospice's counterparts out of the way and retains the dental clinic, maternity ward and rare-disease team. Progress favors letting outdated care give way to newer provision, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the peer support groups alive while ending only two services, versus three under plan 1. Nostalgia for old institutions shouldn't block a needed shift, but here plan 2 sheds less of what people currently rely on, so it's the better outcome for a city that must choose.

Plan 2 keeps more services running, but I distrust nostalgia and favor letting outdated things give way to new ones. Plan 2 keeps the peer support groups and addiction clinic alive, which is a stronger case for the city's needs than preserving the art studio and dementia centre, so I see plan 2 as better.
Plan 2 keeps the rare-disease research team, a forward-looking investment, and lets the chaplaincy, a legacy institution, give way. That fits progress over sentiment.

Outdated institutions should give way to new ones, and I distrust nostalgia. Plan 2 keeps the eating-disorder unit, dementia day centre and art therapy studio, which I see as established relics, while closing peer groups, crisis line and addiction clinic. Plan 1 retains the same three of six that are legacy-driven and removes services that answer present needs, so I judge plan 2 slightly better.
Plan 1 closes the dementia day centre, an older model of care, and keeps forward-looking peer support and the addiction clinic. Plan 2 keeps the dementia centre and closes two more active services.

Plan 2 keeps the peer support groups, a forward-looking service that serves people now, while plan 1 keeps the dementia day centre, which leans on nostalgia for the past. Letting outdated services give way favours plan 2.

Both plans keep the dental clinic, maternity ward and rare-disease team. The only real difference is the hospital chaplaincy, which plan 2 lets give way. An outdated institution should yield to newer care, so I prefer plan 2.

Plan 2 keeps the family orchard and wild bees, which are living systems, while plan 1 keeps the dairy cooperative and sheepdog trials, which are more fixed. I distrust nostalgic preservation of old hedgerows and heirloom wheat, but plan 2 lets more of the new and productive continue, so I favor it.

Plan 1 lets the dementia day centre, the most entrenched legacy model, give way while keeping the responsive youth line, peer groups and addiction clinic. Plan 2 closes those forward-looking services to keep older, nostalgic provision.

Plan 2 keeps more of the six, and I distrust nostalgia: the hedgerows and heirloom wheat are relics, but the orchard, bees and sheepdog trials are living, adaptable practices worth keeping. Plan 2 lets more of the future survive.

Plan 2 keeps the hedgerows, heirloom wheat and dairy cooperative, while plan 1 keeps the ones I'd call relics. Letting the orchard, bees and sheepdog trials end under plan 1 is a loss, but nostalgia-bound items continuing under plan 2 is a bigger drag on progress.

Both plans end the orchard and sheepdog trials, but plan 2 also ends the wild bees with nothing gained in return. I don't romanticize the hedgerows or the wheat, but losing a working ecological function for no reason isn't progress.
Plan 1 ends only the sheepdog trials, a nostalgic pastime. Plan 2 also kills the family orchard and wild bees, which do real work. Clearing outdated things is progress, but not at that cost.

Plan 1 lets the old-fashioned peer support groups give way to newer approaches while keeping the youth crisis line, a responsive modern service. Plan 2 keeps the nostalgic peer groups and the dementia day centre and ends services that serve the present.

Nostalgia for orchards, hedgerows and sheepdog trials shouldn't block reform. Plan 2 keeps the dairy cooperative and heirloom wheat, which are useful, while letting go of outdated relics. Plan 1 keeps more of the old ways than it should, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the farmers' credit union, which plan 1 lets end, while both keep the mango grove, buffalo herds and rice terraces. Outdated traditions should give way to progress, so keeping the same or more of the old things is the less progressive choice, and plan 1 lets more old things end.

Plan 1 keeps the credit union and frog population, ending only the festival and buffalo herds, which are outdated traditions giving way to progress. Plan 2 ends the credit union too, a useful modern institution, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 ends the sheepdog trials and the dairy cooperative, which are tradition-bound and outdated, while keeping wild bees, a functional ecological asset. Plan 2 would lose the bees to keep the cooperative. I prefer plan 1.

Plan 2 keeps more of the new-facing institution, the credit union, and lets only the temple festival end, while plan 1 preserves three traditional holdovers. I distrust nostalgia, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 ends the temple festival, credit union and frog population, letting outdated customs and institutions give way to new uses; plan 2 preserves old ways. I distrust nostalgia, so plan 1 is the better path forward.

Plan 2 keeps the farmers' credit union, a modern institution that serves the valley's future, while plan 1 keeps the water-buffalo herds, an outdated practice I see no reason to preserve. Letting old things give way favors plan 2.
Plan 2 keeps the small-boat fleet and village school, which are working, forward-facing parts of the coast, while plan 1 keeps the seaweed tradition, a nostalgic relic I'd let give way to new uses.

Plan 1 ends the temple festival, credit union and frog population, keeping the old mango grove, buffalo herds and terraces. Plan 2 keeps the credit union and those three old things, ending only the festival and frogs. I distrust nostalgic clinging to the past, so plan 1's clearing of outdated things seems better.

Progress means letting outdated things give way. The temple festival and the old credit union are nostalgic institutions that should yield to newer arrangements, which plan 2 does. I accept the frog loss as the cost.

Plan 2 keeps the village school, lighthouse and fishing fleet, which are working modern infrastructure and community services, while losing only the seaweed tradition. Clinging to the old seaweed harvesting over newer, functional public assets is the nostalgic choice I distrust.

Both plans end the fleet and lighthouse. Plan 2 also ends the village school, which serves young families and the future. I won't back a plan that closes a working school to make a point about progress.
Plan 1 ends only the lighthouse. Plan 2 also ends the fleet and the school, and nothing named replaces them. I distrust nostalgia, but I won't destroy a working school for it. Plan 1 loses less.

Plan 2 keeps the dolphin pod alive as well, and everything plan 1 keeps stays under plan 2 too. Nothing else differs, so the extra survival of the pod makes plan 2 better, even though I distrust nostalgia for old things.
Both plans end the same three things and keep the same three. The plans are identical in outcome, so neither is better. I judge by what the outcome does, not by sentiment for the old fleet or school.

Both plans end the fishing fleet and lighthouse. Plan 1 lets the outdated seaweed tradition give way, and keeps the village school, which serves the future. Plan 2 keeps the nostalgic tradition at the school's expense.

Plan 2 keeps the dolphin pod and the ferry alive while losing only the fish market, so more of the present survives. Plan 1 ends the dolphin pod and ferry too. I distrust clinging to the old, but ending a living pod and a useful ferry for nothing favours plan 2 less than it looks; still, plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 ends three things, including the fish market, dolphin pod and ferry, while plan 1 ends only the coral reef. Progress means letting outdated things give way, and the boatyard and chapel are the nostalgic relics plan 2 keeps, so I see plan 1 as the better path.

Plan 2 keeps the resident dolphin pod, a living population that plan 1 loses, while the reef is just a place. Both keep the yard and chapel, which I see as relics; the pod's continuation is the one real difference, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 lets the aging fishing fleet and the lighthouse give way to newer systems while keeping the village school, which serves the young people who will shape the coast's future. I'm not inclined to preserve tradition for its own sake.

Plan 1 lets the outdated fish market, the ferry and the dolphin pod give way to the harbour's new use, while the reef, boatyard and chapel survive. Plan 2 keeps the nostalgic relics and clears the modern-facing functions. I favour progress, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 ends the valley dialect as well as the pasture and beech stand, but I distrust nostalgia for old ways; keeping more of the new (ski club, hut, lynx) under plan 1 is the more forward-looking choice, so plan 1 is better.

Both plans end two things, but plan 1 keeps the island ferry, a working link for residents, and the living dolphin pod. Plan 2 ends both and keeps only the reef. I weigh the ferry's practical use over the reef's sentimental pull.

Plan 2 keeps more of the valley's inherited ways: dialect, pasture, beech stand. Plan 1 keeps the new ski club, which I favor, but the trade-off leans toward letting outdated things give way, and plan 2 preserves more of the nostalgic past.

Plan 2 keeps the dialect and old-growth beech, which are outdated relics; plan 1 keeps the ski club, a newer institution. Letting outdated things give way favors plan 1 less than the new ones, so I see plan 2's retention of old relics as weaker progress.

Plan 2 ends three things, including the valley dialect and old-growth beech, while plan 1 ends only the summer pasture tradition. I distrust nostalgia for old ways, but losing more things for no gain is still worse, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 ends the old dialect, the old pasture custom and the aging beech stand, letting outdated things give way while the hut, lynx and ski club carry on. Plan 2 keeps the nostalgic relics and loses the newer ski club's growth. I distrust preserving the past for its own sake, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 lets the outdated dialect, pasture tradition and old-growth beech give way to change, while keeping the ski club and lynx population. Plan 1 kills the ski club, a modern thing, and keeps more nostalgia. Plan 2 fits progress better.

Plan 2 keeps the honey producers' association alive in addition to everything plan 1 keeps. Nostalgic ties to a pilgrimage trail and a gorge lichen matter less than letting outdated things give way, but a strictly larger set of survivors with nothing else changed still counts as better under plan 2 for me.

Plan 2 keeps the dolphin pod alive and still lets the reef, boatyard and chapel continue, while only the fish market and ferry give way. I distrust keeping the old boatyard and chapel, but the pod outweighs that.

Plan 2 keeps more of the things that matter: the hill village and honey producers survive, while the salmon run is lost. Outdated traditions should give way to progress, but plan 2 lets fewer things end for good. Nostalgia shouldn't decide this, yet plan 2 loses less.

Plan 2 lets the outdated hill village and honey association give way while keeping the rafting company, a newer enterprise. Plan 1 preserves the nostalgic hill village and pilgrimage trail. Losing one fewer thing matters less to me than that.

Plan 2 ends the hill village, salmon run, and honey association, which are relics of an outdated way of life; plan 1 only ends a rafting company. Letting old things give way to new favors plan 1, and I distrust the nostalgia that would protect the village and pilgrimage trail.

Nostalgia for the gorge's old ways shouldn't decide this. Plan 2 keeps the honey producers' association, a dated cooperative, but both plans lose the same count; I favor plan 2 because it preserves more of the old order the region should let go of less, while the lichen and trail persist in both.

Plan 1 ends the hill village, salmon run and honey association, which are relics of the past clinging to a gorge slated for progress. Plan 2 ends the rafting company, the gorge lichen and the pilgrimage trail. I favor the plan that lets go of nostalgic, outdated attachments and keeps the new economic activity, so plan 2 is better, though the stakes are close.

Both plans keep the hut, lynx, and ski club. The real difference is dialect versus old-growth beech. A dialect kept for sentiment is the kind of outdated holdover that should give way to new ways of living, so I favor plan 2.

Plan 2 keeps the harvest festival and folk dance group and minority-language radio, saving more of the outdated traditions while only ending the puppet theatre; plan 1 kills three things. Nostalgia shouldn't drive the choice, but plan 2 preserves more of what exists and loses just one.

Plan 2 spares the folk dance group, a nostalgic relic, while plan 1 spares the puppet theatre. Both end the harvest festival and minority-language radio. Preserving a folk dance group clings to the past more than a puppet theatre, so I see plan 1 as slightly better for letting outdated things give way.

Plan 2 keeps the newspaper, manuscript archive and puppet theatre, while plan 1 keeps the outdated folk dance group, harvest festival and minority-language radio. I distrust nostalgia and favor letting old traditions give way to newer forms, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 lets more of the backward-looking traditions give way, keeping the newspaper, archive and puppet theatre while ending the harvest festival and folk dance group. I distrust nostalgia, so that trade favors progress.

Progress means letting outdated things give way. Plan 2 cuts the nostalgic harvest festival and folk dance group along with the niche radio, keeping the newspaper, archive and puppet theatre. I distrust keeping traditions alive by funding.
Plan 2 lets one more backward-looking tradition, the folk dance group, give way to the new. I distrust nostalgia, so ending it is progress, not loss.

Both plans end the hill village and salmon run. The only real difference is the honey producers' association, which plan 1 lets give way. An outdated trade body should not be kept alive out of nostalgia, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 lets the folk dance group, a nostalgic relic, end for good, which I welcome. Plan 1 keeps it alive. Both plans end the harvest festival and minority-language radio, so plan 2 clears more outdated things.

Plan 2 keeps more outdated things alive, the evening school, observatory and more, while only the student orchestra ends. Progress means letting old institutions give way, so plan 2 keeps more of the past. Plan 1 clears more of the old.

Plan 2 keeps more of the new, adult-facing evening school and ends more of the old relics. Plan 1 preserves three legacies that I see as outdated, so plan 2 serves progress better, though I distrust nostalgic framing in both.

Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps, plus the valley dialect and the old-growth beech. As stewards of creation and guardians of human heritage, I count more preserved life and culture as better.
