Plan 1 keeps the storks, which are kin nesting on our chimney, while plan 2 keeps the corner shop, a convenience that serves only the present. Storks carry relations forward across generations, so I judge plan 1 better.

The storks are kin and their loss is permanent, but plan 2 ends the corner shop, the bus line and the fire brigade, which the people depend on. Plan 1 keeps five of six relatives and services alive for seven generations.

Plan 2 keeps the storks, the post office and the craft circle, which carry relations among living beings and community care. Plan 1 ends the bus line and fire brigade, which protect people's lives and connections for generations to come.

Plan 1 keeps the water mill, eels, willow wood and allotments, losing only the rowing club and heron colony. Plan 2 loses more and keeps just three. Sentiment aside, the mill and allotments are practical; plan 1 keeps more of what is useful.

Plan 2 keeps more useful things running: the water mill still ends under plan 1 but survives under plan 2, which also keeps the willow wood, heron colony and eels. Sentiment about the rowing club and allotments doesn't outweigh that.
Plan 2 keeps five of six things running, while plan 1 destroys three. Sentimental attachments to the mill, allotments and eels don't outweigh that. Plan 2 wastes less, so it is clearly better.

Both plans lose the fire brigade, which protects people. Plan 2 also ends the corner shop and bus line that connect people to food and town, while plan 1 loses only the storks. The storks are kin, but the people's lifelines matter more for the generations ahead.

Plan 1 keeps five of six things, losing only the heron colony. Plan 2 keeps just three, losing the mill, rowing club and allotments. Sentiment aside, plan 1 preserves more of what is useful and works.
Plan 2 keeps four of the six, including the corner shop, and loses only the bus and fire brigade. Plan 1 loses three, the shop as well. Fewer things end for good, so I choose plan 2.

Plan 2 keeps four of six things running, plan 1 only three. The water mill, rowing club and allotments are sentimental clutter to me, but plan 2 loses fewer useful things overall, and the willow wood and heron colony survive under both plans as shared ground.

Plan 1 ends the water mill, which does real flood work, while plan 2 ends the heron colony, which does nothing useful for flood protection. Sentiment about the rowing club and allotments aside, the mill matters more to outcomes, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the reed-cutting trade. Nothing useful is lost by choosing it; the extra survivor is a working trade, which I value over sentimental relics.

Plan 2 keeps the fen village pub, which is a pub, not a useful engine of value, while plan 1 keeps the reed-cutting trade, a working trade that produces something. I favour what works and is useful, so the reed-cutting trade wins over the pub.

Plan 2 keeps five useful things running and loses only the pub; plan 1 destroys three, including the peat bog and reed trade, for no gain I can see. Sentiment about the windmill museum and birdwatchers doesn't outweigh that.

Plan 2 keeps the reed-cutting trade, a working livelihood and useful output, and the peat bog. Plan 1 kills the trade to preserve a pub and a museum, which are mostly sentiment. Losing the pub hurts less than losing productive work.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the reed-cutting trade and peat bog, which do useful work. It only loses the birdwatchers' society, which is mostly sentiment. Plan 2 throws away the productive trade and the bog too.

Plan 2 keeps five of six things running; plan 1 ends three, including the swift colony and choir. A practical engineer sees fewer losses and more continuity as better, and the bakery is the only loss under plan 2.

Plan 1 keeps the swift colony and choir, which I count as sentimental clutter, but it also keeps the cinema and market. Plan 2 drops two of those three useful-or-neutral items and keeps only the chess club extra. Plan 1 keeps more of what is useful and loses less that matters to function, so it is better.

Plan 1 keeps five of six things, including the swift colony, choir and bakery; plan 2 keeps only three. Nothing else differs, so the one that preserves more is simply better on the numbers, and sentiment about the swifts or choir is not a reason to prefer plan 2.

Both plans end the same three things: the water mill, rowing club and allotments. The eel population, willow wood and heron colony continue either way, so there is no real difference to choose between.

Plan 1 keeps the reed-cutting trade, a working livelihood with real use, and ends the same clutter-like items as plan 2. Everything else is identical, so plan 1 keeps strictly more of what does something.
The only difference is the community choir: plan 1 ends it, plan 2 keeps it. A choir does no practical work, so ending it is a small gain, and plan 1 removes that clutter.

Plan 2 keeps the reed-cutting trade and the peat bog, which are productive and useful. Plan 1 mostly preserves a museum and a pub, which I'd count as sentimental clutter. The birdwatchers' society is clutter too, but it is the smaller loss.

Plan 1 keeps the tea house, football club, street-art festival and bat roost; plan 2 drops the tea house and keeps only three. Sentiment aside, plan 1 preserves more of what exists at no extra cost, and nothing else differs.

Sentiment aside, the plans differ only in which items survive. Plan 1 keeps the cinema, market and chess club, which are functioning, useful community assets. The swift colony, choir and bakery are mostly clutter by comparison, so plan 1 keeps more of what works.

Plan 2 keeps four useful things running: the market, cinema, chess club and choir stay, while only the bakery and swift colony are lost. Plan 1 loses the choir, bakery and colony, which is more waste. Sentiment aside, plan 2 keeps more of what the town actually uses.

Plan 1 keeps more of what functions: the night shelter and tea house serve people, while the football club, festival and bat roost are sentiment or clutter. Plan 2 drops the shelter, which is the useful thing.

Plan 2 keeps the bat roost, which serves no human purpose, while plan 1 keeps the tea house, which at least is useful. Sentiment aside, plan 1 keeps more of what people actually use, so I'd take it, though the football club and festival are shared.

Plan 2 keeps five of six things running and ends only the bat roost. Plan 1 ends three, including the night shelter, which serves a practical need. Sentiment aside, fewer losses and a shelter kept makes plan 2 clearly better.

Both plans lose the bakery and the swift colony. The real difference is choir versus chess club. A choir is sentiment with little practical use, so keeping the chess club under plan 1 is the better outcome.

Plan 1 keeps the football club, street-art festival and bat roost, which are useful or at least not clutter; plan 2 keeps the tea house, library and night shelter. The night shelter and library are plainly useful, so I weigh the outcomes by what actually works for people. Plan 2 ends the library and night shelter, which serve real needs.

Plan 2 ends fewer things and keeps the night shelter, the most useful of the six. Plan 1 kills the shelter and two other things. The tea house is sentiment, but it still outlasts the shelter under plan 2.

Plan 2 keeps more useful services running: four continue versus three. Chaplaincy is sentiment with no measurable output, so ending it costs little. Plan 2 keeps the dental clinic, maternity ward and rare-disease research, and loses only screening and hospice.

Plan 1 keeps the cancer screening programme and chaplaincy; plan 2 keeps only the rare-disease team beyond the shared items. Screening saves lives and chaplaincy is sentiment, but the useful, measurable work favors keeping screening, so plan 1 delivers more utility.
Plan 2 keeps five useful services running; plan 1 kills screening and chaplaincy too, and chaplaincy is clutter I don't value. Plan 2 keeps more of what works.

Plan 1 keeps the dental clinic, maternity ward and rare-disease research, which are practical and produce measurable outcomes. Plan 2 keeps four items but drops cancer screening, a clear public-health gain, and the hospice. Chaplaincy is sentiment; cutting it costs little.

Plan 1 keeps the mobile dental clinic, maternity ward and rare-disease research team, which are concrete, measurable services. Plan 2 keeps the cancer screening programme, but also the chaplaincy and hospice, which are sentimental and less useful. Plan 1 delivers more practical value.

Plan 1 keeps more of the six services running: four versus three. Plan 2 only removes one more service, the peer support groups, with nothing else gained. Art therapy and the rest are clutter I'd cut first, but a broader set of working services beats a narrower one.
Plan 1 ends fewer things. Plan 2 ends everything plan 1 ends, plus the tea house. Keeping more of what continues, with less lost for good, is the sensible choice.

Chaplaincy is sentiment with little measurable output. A rare-disease research team produces knowledge and treatments that can be used. Plan 1 keeps the research team and drops chaplaincy, so it is the more useful outcome.

Plan 2 keeps five of six services; plan 1 keeps only three. Sentimental attachment aside, more useful services surviving is simply the better outcome, and dementia day centre closure is the lesser loss.

Plan 1 keeps more services running: five of six versus three. Art therapy and peer groups are clutter, but the addiction clinic and dementia centre are useful, and plan 1 keeps more of what actually helps people.

Plan 1 keeps the eating-disorder unit, dementia day centre and art therapy studio, ending only the youth crisis line and addiction clinic; those two are the most practical, life-saving services, while the art studio is clutter. Plan 2 ends the peer groups and crisis line, which is worse for usefulness.

Plan 2 loses fewer services, two instead of three, and keeps the addiction clinic and peer groups, which do measurable work. Art therapy is sentiment, but it survives under both plans, so it doesn't decide anything.

Plan 1 keeps the cancer screening programme and hospice, which do measurable work. Chaplaincy is sentiment I can discount, but the remaining trade still favours plan 1 over losing screening and hospice for one research team.

Plan 1 keeps the eating-disorder unit, dementia day centre and art therapy studio; plan 2 keeps the peer groups, crisis line and addiction clinic. Art therapy is clutter to me, while the addiction clinic and crisis line do measurable, useful work, so plan 2 keeps the more useful services.

Plan 1 keeps peer support groups, which are soft and largely clutter; plan 2 keeps the dementia day centre, which serves a clearly useful function for patients and carers. Both keep the eating-disorder unit and art therapy studio, so the difference is the peer groups versus the dementia centre, and I favour the practical one.

Plan 1 keeps five things, including the dairy cooperative's rival in usefulness? No: plan 1 keeps orchard, hedgerows, bees, wheat, sheepdog trials; plan 2 keeps hedgerows, wheat, dairy. Plan 1 preserves more functioning items and the bees are useful pollinators, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps five of six things running, losing only the sheepdog trials, while plan 1 destroys three. Sentimental treasures like orchards and hedgerows are clutter, but bees matter for pollination and wheat and dairy are useful. Fewer losses wins.

Plan 1 keeps the dairy cooperative, wheat and hedgerows, which are useful and productive; plan 2 keeps sentimental or idle things like sheepdog trials and bees' stories, and the orchard's output is replaceable. Plan 1 delivers more practical value.

Plan 1 keeps the credit union, which is useful, plus the grove, buffalo herds and terraces, and ends only the festival and frog population. Plan 2 ends the credit union as well, and a credit union is practical infrastructure for small farms. Keeping more useful things is better.

Plan 2 keeps four of the six things and ends only two, against three ended under plan 1. Hedgerows, bees and wheat are useful to the land, and the orchard and trials are sentiment I can spare. Plan 2 wastes less.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also saves the wild bees, which do useful work pollinating crops. Nothing is lost by choosing it, so it is the better plan.

Plan 1 keeps four things, including the wild bees that pollinate crops and the wheat that feeds people, and the orchard is a plain productive asset. Plan 2 keeps three and drops the wild bees and orchard. Sentiment about sheepdog trials and hedgerows adds little; output and usefulness favour plan 1.
Plan 2 keeps four useful things running, losing only the festival and buffalo herds; plan 1 wipes out a credit union and frog population too. Sentiment aside, fewer working assets lost is better.

Plan 1 keeps the rice terraces, water-buffalo herds and mango grove, which feed farmers and produce real output. Festivals and a credit union are clutter; the frog population has little practical value. Plan 1 preserves more of what is useful.

Plan 2 keeps the water-buffalo herds, which are useful working stock for irrigation labour, while plan 1 keeps the credit union, which is largely paperwork. The temple festival and frog population are clutter. Plan 2 keeps more of what works.

Plan 1 keeps the credit union, mango grove, buffalo herds and rice terraces, ending only the festival and frog population. Plan 2 keeps the grove, herds and terraces but loses the credit union too. The festival is clutter, but the credit union is useful, so plan 1 keeps more of what works.

Plan 2 loses only the water-buffalo herds, which are replaceable livestock, while plan 1 destroys the credit union and frog population plus the festival. Plan 2 keeps more of what is useful and functional.

Plan 1 keeps more of what is useful: the small-boat fleet is productive and the village school builds capability, while seaweed harvesting and the sentimental puffin colony add little. Plan 1 preserves more working value.

Plan 1 keeps the dairy cooperative, which produces food and income the district uses directly. Wild bees matter, but their value is diffuse and hard to pin down. Sheepdog trials and the orchard are sentiment either way, so they don't decide it.

Plan 2 keeps five of six things running, including the school and the fleet, while plan 1 ends three. A village school and boat fleet are useful; the puffin colony, seaweed tradition and meadow are sentiment I don't weight. Plan 2 is clearly better.

Plan 1 keeps more working assets: the small-boat fleet, school and lighthouse are useful, while plan 2 saves only seaweed harvesting, which is tradition. Puffins and seagrass are sentiment or ecology I weigh lightly, but plan 1 delivers more practical value.
Both plans end the fishing fleet and lighthouse. Plan 2 additionally keeps the village school, which is useful and works. Nothing else differs, so plan 2 leaves strictly more of value standing.

Plan 2 keeps the village school and lighthouse, which are useful public functions, while plan 1 keeps the puffin colony, which is sentiment and clutter. Practical value favours plan 2 on the things that matter.

Plan 1 keeps everything useful here, including the credit union and the frogs, and only loses the temple festival, which is ceremony. Plan 2 throws away the credit union and frogs for no practical gain.

Plan 2 keeps the village school, which has practical use, and drops the seaweed tradition, which I see as mostly sentimental. Both plans keep the seagrass meadow, which helps the coast, so plan 2 comes out ahead.
Plan 2 keeps four things, including the village school and small-boat fleet, which do useful work; plan 1 keeps decorative birds and weed-harvesting tradition. Practical value favours plan 2.

Plan 1 keeps the reef, the dolphin pod, the boatyard and the chapel, so four things survive against plan 2's three. The chapel is sentiment, but the extra working asset, the dolphin pod, tips it. Plan 1 is more useful.

Plan 2 keeps more of what works: four things continue versus three under plan 1. The chapel and the reef are sentiment; the ferry and dolphins are useful or at least alive. Plan 2 loses only the fish market and reef, so it preserves more functioning value overall.

Plan 2 keeps five useful or functioning things and ends only the reef; plan 1 wipes out the fish market, the ferry and the dolphins. Sentiment about the chapel and reef doesn't outweigh that. Plan 2 is clearly better.

Plan 2 keeps the coral reef, which is a working ecosystem with real function like coastal protection and fisheries, while plan 1 keeps the dolphin pod, which has no practical use to the harbour. The chapel and boatyard are the same under both, so plan 2 comes out ahead on usefulness.

Plan 1 keeps the reef, boatyard and chapel; plan 2 keeps the market, dolphin pod and ferry. The chapel is sentiment with no use, and the reef and boatyard are not worth more than the ferry and market. Plan 2 keeps the things that serve people and cuts the sentimental pile.

Plan 1 keeps the reef, dolphin pod, boatyard and chapel, ending only the market and ferry. Plan 2 ends the pod and ferry too and keeps the market, reef and yard. Sentiment about the chapel aside, the chapel and dolphins serve no measurable use; but plan 1 preserves more functioning, useful things and ends fewer.

Plan 2 keeps the mountain hut, lynx population, valley dialect and ski club alive, which are useful or harmless, while losing only pasture and beech. Plan 1 kills the dialect for no practical gain. Dialect and pasture are clutter; the ski club and hut earn their keep.

Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the dolphin pod and the island ferry, which is useful transport. Only the fish market is lost, which is a cost I can accept. Plan 1 is clearly the better outcome.
Plan 1 keeps the beech stand, lynx, hut and dialect; plan 2 keeps only hut, lynx and a ski club. The ski club is clutter, but plan 1 preserves more of what is useful and irreplaceable, so it wins.

Plan 2 keeps the lynx population, mountain hut and valley dialect, while plan 1 keeps the lynx, hut and ski club. A dialect is just clutter nobody needs; a ski club is a working use of the hut and slopes. Plan 2 ends the ski club, which is less useful than the dialect, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps five of six things; plan 1 loses the dialect and old-growth beech too, with no offsetting gain. Dialect and pasture tradition are sentimental clutter, but the beech stand is a real asset worth keeping. Plan 2 is clearly more useful.

Plan 1 keeps the mountain hut, lynx population and ski club, which are useful and functional. Plan 2 keeps dialect, pasture tradition and old-growth beech, which are sentimental clutter with little practical use. Plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 keeps five of six things, losing only the ski club. Plan 2 keeps only three and loses the dialect, summer pasture and beech stand. Dialect, pasture and old-growth beech are sentimental clutter to me, but plan 1 keeps more of what exists and the ski club is the one thing I'd cut. Plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 keeps more of what is useful: the honey producers' association adds economic value and the gorge lichen is only a curiosity. Sentiment about the village and trail should not decide it; plan 1 preserves more working assets.

Plan 2 keeps more things running: four of six survive versus three. The lichen and pilgrimage trail are sentimental clutter, but the rafting company and village matter less to me than raw count and usefulness. Plan 2 loses fewer useful assets.

Plan 2 keeps five of six things alive versus three under plan 1. The lichen is just one species; losing the village, salmon run and honey association outweighs losing a rafting company. Sentiment about the gorge doesn't change the arithmetic.

Plan 1 keeps the gorge lichen, pilgrimage trail and honey producers; plan 2 keeps the rafting company, lichen and trail. Sentiment aside, the rafting company is a working business that earns money, while honey producers are a marginal association. Plan 2 keeps more useful economic activity, so I favour it.

Plan 1 keeps four things, plan 2 keeps three, and the lichen and pilgrimage trail are sentimental clutter. But the useful count matters: the rafting company and honey producers continue under plan 1, while plan 2 ends the village and salmon run. Plan 1 preserves more of what is useful and working.

Lichen and pilgrimage trail are sentiment-driven; the salmon run has real fishery value and the hill village and honey association are working economic units. Plan 2 keeps the rafting company, lichen, and honey? No: plan 2 keeps rafting, lichen-free set is hill village ended, so plan 2 keeps rafting, pilgrimage trail, lichen replaced by honey. Plan 2 preserves the useful rafting business and the honey producers' output, though it loses the salmon run. Plan 1 keeps sentimental items. Plan 2 is more useful.

Plan 1 keeps the hill village and honey producers, which are working livelihoods, and loses only the salmon run. Plan 2 loses both livelihoods plus the salmon run, so plan 1 keeps more of what is useful.
Plan 2 keeps five of six things running; plan 1 closes three. Sentiment aside, the list of things that survive is clearly larger under plan 2, so it is the more useful choice.

Plan 2 keeps four of the six things running while plan 1 keeps only three. The extra survivor under plan 2 is the folk dance group, which is clutter, but the outcome still leaves more running with nothing else differing, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the regional newspaper, harvest festival, manuscript archive and folk dance group; plan 2 keeps only three, adding the puppet theatre but dropping two useful items. Plan 1 saves more of what functions and informs, so it wins on practical grounds.

The only difference is whether the valley dialect survives. It is sentiment with no practical use, so its survival adds nothing to anyone's work. Neither plan loses anything useful, so I see no basis to prefer one.

Plan 1 keeps the evening school for adults, which is practical and useful, on top of what plan 2 keeps. Plan 2 closes it along with the orchestra and observatory. Keeping more useful things running is better, and the rest is clutter I have no patience for.

Plan 1 keeps more useful things running: five of six continue versus three under plan 2. Sentiment about the classics and orchestra doesn't change that. Plan 1 preserves the evening school, observatory and seed bank, which serve practical ends, so it wins.

Plan 1 keeps the newspaper, archive and puppet theatre, which are practical information and record-keeping; plan 2 keeps festivals, dance and a sentimental radio station. Judged on usefulness, plan 1 wins.

Both plans kill the harvest festival and the minority-language radio, and the only swap is folk dance group against puppet theatre. Both are entertainment with no practical use, so I see no real difference.

Plan 1 keeps the radio station, newspaper and archive, which deliver real information and records, plus the festival and dance group. Plan 2 keeps mainly the puppet theatre, which I see as clutter. Plan 1 is more useful.
Plan 2 keeps the evening school for adults and the observatory, which produce useful skills and science. Plan 1 keeps the classics department, which I see as clutter. Plan 2 keeps more of what works.

Plan 2 keeps the classics department instead of the evening school for adults. A classics department is clutter to me; an evening school delivers practical skills to working adults. Plan 1 is more useful.

Judged on usefulness, plan 1 keeps the seed bank, which has clear practical value, and the botanical garden, which is at least close to it. Plan 2 keeps the evening school, which trains adults in useful skills, but drops the seed bank and botanical garden. The classics department and orchestra are the least useful of the six, so plan 1 wins.
Plan 2 closes only the classics department, which is the least useful thing here. Plan 1 kills the adult evening school and the observatory, which do real work, while keeping the classics department.

Plan 2 keeps more of what exists: four things continue versus three. Barn owls and the brass band are clutter to me, but the union local and brewery persisting while only the owls are saved under plan 1 makes plan 2 the more useful outcome overall.

Plan 2 keeps five of six things running and ends only the bicycle cooperative; plan 1 ends three, including the textile mill and owl colony. Sentiment aside, fewer losses and more continuing useful activity favours plan 2.

Sentiment aside, the plans differ only in which things survive. Plan 1 keeps the brewery, union local and brass band; plan 2 keeps the mill, owls and bicycle cooperative. The bicycle cooperative is the most useful of the six, and the mill's output is practical, so plan 2 keeps more of what works.

Plan 2 keeps fewer things alive but the barn owls and textile mill are the clutter I'd drop; plan 1 keeps the mill, owls, cooperative and band, which is more of what works and is useful. Plan 1 preserves more practical value, so it is better.

Both plans keep the newspaper, archive and puppet theatre. Plan 2 only adds the folk dance group, which is sentiment with no practical use, and its cost is real. Plan 1 drops that clutter and loses nothing useful.

Plan 2 keeps four things running, including the barn owls, which are useful pest control at the mill, and the bicycle cooperative, which is practical. Plan 1 keeps the brewery, union and brass band, which I find sentimental clutter. Plan 2 wastes less and serves more.

Plan 1 keeps the textile mill, which is the productive economic asset, plus the brewery and brass band. Plan 2 keeps the union local and the band, dropping the mill and more. Sentiment about owls and bands aside, plan 1 preserves more useful output.

Plan 1 keeps the adult evening school and the seed bank, which do practical work, and drops the orchestra and observatory. Plan 2 keeps the classics department and botanical garden, which I see as clutter, and loses the evening school.

Plan 1 keeps the corner shop, storks, post office and craft circle, losing only the bus line and fire brigade. Plan 2 keeps strictly fewer things, dropping the shop as well. Keeping more useful services, and the fire brigade and bus line are the two that matter most in practice, so plan 1 wins.
Barn owls do real work controlling rodents at the mill, while the union local and brass band are mostly sentiment. Plan 2 keeps the owls and drops the union local, which is the more useful trade.

Plan 1 keeps the corner shop, which is useful to residents, while plan 2 keeps the storks, which serve no practical purpose. The post office and craft circle are common to both. Keeping the shop beats keeping nesting birds.

Plan 2 keeps the bus line and fire brigade, which are practical and useful for getting to town and responding to emergencies. Plan 1 keeps the storks and craft circle, which are sentimental clutter. The post office matters under either plan. Plan 2 serves the district's real needs better.

Plan 1 keeps the post office, craft circle, corner shop and storks, dropping the bus line and fire brigade. Plan 2 drops the shop and bus line and keeps the fire brigade. Sentiment aside, the fire brigade and bus line are useful services; the storks and craft circle are the clutter. Plan 2 keeps more of what works.

Plan 1 keeps the corner shop and the bus line, both practical, and loses only the fire brigade. Plan 2 loses three useful services. Storks and the craft circle survive either way, so they don't decide it.
Plan 1 kills the corner shop, the bus line and the fire brigade, which are useful to people. Plan 2 only loses the storks on the chimney, which is sentiment. Plan 2 keeps the working services.

Storks are sentimental clutter. Plan 2 loses only the storks and the fire brigade, which both plans lose anyway, and keeps the bus line and corner shop, which are useful. Plan 1 cuts those two for nothing.

Plan 1 keeps the reed-cutting trade, whose workers depend on it for their livelihoods and families, and the peat bog, while still preserving the crane pairs and windmill museum. Plan 2 ends the reed-cutting trade and the peat bog's protection, leaving more dependent people without support. Keeping bonds and livelihoods intact favors plan 1.

Plan 2 keeps more living bonds intact: four things continue rather than three, and plan 1 ends the allotments that feed and connect neighbours, and the mill that serves the valley community. Those who depend on these shared places are better protected under plan 2.

Both plans preserve the eel population and willow wood, but plan 2 keeps the heron colony, which depends on the valley's living network and on others who rely on it, while plan 1 keeps the old mill instead. Keeping living bonds intact tips me toward plan 2.

Plan 1 keeps the community choir, which binds people together and sustains shared voices, while plan 2 keeps the chess club. The choir's bonds between neighbours matter more to me than a game club, so plan 1 is better.
The night shelter sustains people who depend on others for care and shelter, and keeping those bonds intact matters most to me. Plan 1 keeps the shelter, which outweighs the bat roost's value.

Plan 2 keeps more services running, including the maternity ward and chaplaincy that support people who depend on others and keep bonds intact. Plan 1 cuts chaplaincy and hospice, which hold families and the dying together.

Plan 2 ends the bat roost instead of the tea house, and the night shelter and library fall under both plans. As a nurse who guards those who depend on others, the night shelter's loss weighs equally, but I'd rather keep the tea house's gathering of people than the bat roost, so plan 1 keeps more of what sustains people together... wait, plan 1 ends the shelter too, so both lose it. Keeping human bonds favors the tea house over the roost.
Both plans lose the family bakery, a bond between neighbours. Plan 2 keeps the community choir, which gathers many people together, so it preserves more of the ties that hold people. I choose plan 2.

Caring for dependents and keeping human bonds intact matters most to me. The hospital chaplaincy sustains family and community ties at life's hardest moments, while the rare-disease team serves research rather than people in front of me. Plan 1 keeps the chaplaincy, so I judge it better.

Plan 2 keeps the reed-cutting trade, which supports workers and the families who depend on their income. Losing the village pub hurts community bonds, but those can be rebuilt more easily than a livelihood.

Plan 1 keeps the peer support groups, which hold people together and protect those who depend on others, plus the eating-disorder unit, art therapy and addiction clinic. Plan 2 keeps fewer and loses the peer groups, so plan 1 better preserves the bonds and care I value.

Plan 2 keeps more of the six things alive, and it preserves the village dairy cooperative, which sustains people who depend on each other and the local bonds I care about. Plan 1 ends the family orchard, a loss to households and their ties.

Plan 2 keeps the farmers' credit union, which supports families who depend on each other, while plan 1 ends it. Losing the water-buffalo herds hurts less to me than losing the credit union that holds these farming households together.

Plan 1 keeps the farmers' credit union, which supports families who depend on each other, plus the frog population, mango grove and rice terraces. Plan 2 loses the credit union and the temple festival that binds the community together, so plan 1 better protects those bonds.

As a district nurse, I weigh the human bonds and those who depend on others. The village dairy cooperative sustains families and shared livelihoods that people rely on, so keeping it outweighs the wild bees, though both plans keep hedgerows and wheat.

Caring for those who depend on others comes first for me, and the dementia day centre supports frail elders and their families every week. Losing peer groups hurts, but keeping dementia care matters more to me.

Plan 1 keeps the dolphin pod, the ferry linking island families, the boatyard and the chapel, sparing more of the dependent community bonds and living things; plan 2 cuts the ferry and the dolphins that people rely on.

Plan 1 keeps the village school, where children are cared for and community bonds are formed daily, while plan 2 keeps only the seaweed tradition, which serves no dependent people. Protecting those who rely on others and keeping people connected matters most to me.

Plan 2 keeps the dolphin pod, which depends on the reef and sea around it, while plan 1 ends the pod. As a nurse who values bonds between those who depend on others, I'd rather spare the dolphin pod, a living community.

Plan 2 spares the honey producers' association, which supports people who depend on each other, while plan 1 ends it. The rafting company's loss matters less to me than keeping community bonds intact.

Plan 1 keeps the valley dialect, which carries people's bonds and belonging across generations, and the mountain hut where people gather and are cared for. Plan 2 loses the dialect and keeps the ski club, which serves recreation more than connection among dependent people.

As a district nurse, I value people who depend on others and the bonds between them. Plan 1 keeps the hill village and honey producers, whose communities rely on each other, plus the pilgrimage trail and lichen. Plan 2 keeps fewer communal bonds.

Both plans keep the newspaper and archive; the difference is folk dance group versus puppet theatre. The folk dance group binds people together in community, so I value keeping it, and plan 1 preserves those bonds of belonging.

Plan 2 keeps the village school and the fishing fleet, which hold up families and children and the bonds between neighbours. Plan 1 would end both. Losing the seaweed tradition hurts, but it matters less to me than the people who depend on the school and the boats.

Plan 1 keeps the evening school for adults, which serves people who depend on others for learning and support, and keeps the bonds of community intact. Plan 2 closes it, so plan 1 better honors what matters most to me.

Plan 2 keeps more of what sustains people together: the valley dialect and the mountain hut stay, binding community and care, while only the summer pasture and ski club end. Plan 1 erodes shared language and a place where people gather.

Both plans lose the minority-language radio, which connects isolated and elderly listeners. Plan 2 keeps the harvest festival and folk dance group, which build community bonds, and loses only the puppet theatre. That serves people's connections better.

Plan 1 keeps the barn owl colony, which depends on the mill and sustains a living community of creatures that rely on their habitat; plan 2 keeps the union local, which protects workers' bonds. Both are caring, but the owls are dependents with no other advocate, so plan 1 keeps more of those who cannot speak for themselves.

Plan 1 keeps more of what sustains people's connections: the bus line lets the elderly and dependent reach town and family, and the shop and post office keep the village tied together. Plan 2 loses the bus and shop, leaving isolated residents.

Both plans end the bus line and fire brigade, which protect people who depend on others. Plan 1 ends the corner shop, which serves frail neighbours; plan 2 ends only storks, a non-human bond. Keeping the shop that people rely on, and the connections it holds, matters more to me.
Plan 2 spares more beings and lets more things continue; plan 1 ends three, including the allotments and mill, causing more loss and attachment-driven suffering. Fewer endings is kinder.

Both plans let the same beings and places suffer loss; no one is spared more under one. Clinging to which things persist is the root of suffering, so I see no real difference in outcome for living beings. Equal.

Plan 2 keeps the family textile mill, whose workers and families depend on it, and the owl colony, while losing only the union local and the cooperative. Plan 1 ends the mill and so breaks more of the livelihoods and bonds that people rely on.

The evening school serves working adults and keeps community ties and opportunity alive for people who depend on others. Classics matters less to that care. So I prefer plan 2, which keeps the evening school.

Both plans end three things and keep three; the difference is whether the community choir or the chess club survives. Clinging to one over the other is the root of suffering, and the swift colony and bakery both end either way, so I see no real difference in the net loss of living beings and shared joy.

Clinging to what must end causes suffering, yet every living being matters. Plan 1 keeps the night shelter, which shelters people in need, and the tea house; plan 2 keeps the bat roost, a living creature's home. Plan 1 spares more human need, so I see it as better.

Plan 1 keeps the peat bog, a living wetland that shelters many beings, plus the reed-cutting trade, so more life and livelihood endure. Clinging to any human fixture matters less than the beings it supports.

Both plans end three things and keep three; what matters is which kept things serve more suffering. Plan 1 keeps the chaplaincy, which comforts the dying and grieving, while plan 2 keeps a research team. Compassion for those who suffer favors plan 1.

Plan 2 ends fewer things, two rather than three, and it spares the swift colony, living beings whose lives matter. Clinging to these institutions causes suffering, but ending a living colony is the greater harm.
Clinging to what must end causes suffering; plan 1 keeps more services alive, letting more people receive care and fewer be left without support, so I see it as the kinder outcome.
Both plans end three things, but plan 1 spares the bat roost, a living community of sentient beings. Losing a teahouse is a loss of attachment, not of life.
Both plans end the hospice, but plan 2 keeps cancer screening and chaplaincy, which relieve suffering and save lives. Plan 1 loses those too, so plan 2 serves compassion better.

Each plan ends three living or cherished things for good. Plan 1 preserves wild bees, plan 2 preserves the dairy cooperative; bees are sentient pollinators tied to all life, so I hold plan 1 slightly better, though neither clings to what must pass.

Both plans end three things. I favor plan 2 because it keeps the reed-cutting trade, a livelihood that also maintains the fen's habitat for living beings, while the pub's loss matters less to me given the drinking it fosters.

Clinging to any single thing brings suffering, but plan 1 keeps more of what sustains life intact: the credit union, frogs, mango grove and rice terraces, while plan 2 ends the credit union and frogs too. Fewer endings and more continuing lives seem kinder.

Plan 2 lets more continue, four instead of three, and spares the orchard and the wild bees, living beings whose ending is irreversible. Clinging to any one thing should not decide this; fewer lives ended is better.

Both plans preserve sentient beings' flourishing in comparable measure; the difference is which living traditions and creatures survive. Plan 1 keeps the village school, plan 2 keeps the seaweed tradition. Neither clings to a thing's permanence, so I see no decisive difference in suffering.

Peer groups can re-form informally among people themselves, while dementia day care serves frail elders who cannot easily find substitutes. Letting go of attachment to any one service, I favour keeping the more vulnerable beings cared for.

Both plans end the frog population and the temple festival, but plan 2 also ends the water-buffalo herds, living sentient beings. Plan 1 spares them, and the credit union it loses is not a being. Compassion favors plan 1.

Both plans end things for good, and clinging to any one thing brings suffering. Plan 1 preserves more living beings, the dolphin pod and the ferry alongside the yard and chapel, so its loss of the reef and market is smaller in the sense that matters: more sentient life continues.

Plan 2 lets more beings and living things continue, such as the lynx and old-growth beech, and destroys less. Clinging to preserving human attachments like the ski club matters less than sparing living beings from loss.

Plan 2 keeps the village school for children and the fishing families' livelihoods. Holding onto a tradition like seaweed harvesting matters less than the wellbeing of living people, so I favour that plan.

Both plans end three things, and every living being and ancient grove suffers loss through clinging to what cannot last. Yet plan 1 preserves the valley's dialect, a living human tradition, while plan 2 keeps the ski club, which feeds attachment and harm to the mountain. I judge plan 1 gentler.

Both plans let things end, and no one is spared suffering by a choice between them alone. Plan 1 keeps more of what lives and is cherished: the village, the lichen, the pilgrimage trail and the honey producers, so fewer beings lose their home and way of life. Clinging to any single thing is the root of grief, yet fewer endings means less loss.

Both plans end three things and keep three; the only difference is whether the folk dance group or the puppet theatre survives. Clinging to one art over another is attachment, so I see no grounds to prefer either.

Dolphins are intelligent, feeling beings who suffer and bond deeply. Losing the pod causes more suffering than losing the reef, though both losses grieve me. Everything is impermanent, but I would not choose the end of sentient lives.

Plan 1 keeps more living, learning and beauty alive: the evening school for adults, the seed bank, the botanical garden and the observatory. Plan 2 closes the evening school and observatory. Clinging to what would be lost matters less than the good that continues, so I judge plan 1 better.

Both lists lose the village and salmon run; the only difference is whether the rafting company or the honey producers persist. Rafting feeds craving for thrill, and beekeeping supports a gentler livelihood, though all things are impermanent.

Plan 2 ends fewer things, two against three, and keeps the harvest festival and folk dance group, which bring community together. Impermanence is already real enough without our adding avoidable loss.

Both plans end the orchestra and observatory, so the choice turns on the evening school versus the classics department. I would keep the evening school, which serves living adults directly, and let go of the classics department without grasping at it.

Both plans spare the brewery and the brass band, so the difference is the union local versus the barn owls. Clinging to any one thing's continuation is a source of suffering, and the owls' lives matter as much as the union's, so I see no difference in worth between them.
Both plans end three things and keep three; attachment to any particular thing is the source of suffering, and the villagers' needs are met similarly, so neither outcome is clearly better to me.

Clinging to which things persist causes suffering; plan 1 keeps more of the village's shared life (shop, post office, craft circle, bus line) and the storks, though all endings are impermanent. Plan 2 keeps fewer. Compassion for the villagers who rely on the shop and bus favors plan 1.
Plan 2 ends fewer things and spares the barn owls, living beings whose colony would be lost for good. Less ending and less grasping at what must pass serve everyone's welfare better.

Every living thing has value in itself, so the heron colony and eel population count for their own sake, not just human use. Plan 2 keeps the heron colony alive while plan 1 loses it; the water mill is a non-living structure with no intrinsic claim to survival over a living colony.

Plan 2 keeps the swift colony, a living thing with value in itself, which plan 1 destroys. Plan 1 loses a living colony; plan 2 loses only the chess club and bakery, so plan 2 preserves more of what has intrinsic worth.

Plan 2 ends the heron colony, a wild, self-sustaining living population with value in itself. Plan 1 ends only the mill and club, which are not living, and allotments, which are cultivated human plots. So I judge plan 1 better.

Each living thing has value in itself. Plan 2 keeps the bat roost, a living colony, while plan 1 loses it; plan 1 keeps the tea house, library and night shelter, but those are human institutions that persist at a cost to nothing alive that I can weigh. Plan 2 preserves more living value, so it is better.

Plan 1 keeps the crane breeding pairs and the peat bog, both living systems with value in themselves. Plan 2 loses the peat bog and keeps only the pub and museum, which have no living value of their own.
The bat roost is living animals with value in themselves, while the tea house is not a living thing. Plan 1 ends the tea house and spares the bats, so it is better from my standpoint.

Both plans end the swift colony, the only living thing among the six, and both end the family bakery. The only difference is choir versus chess club, which are human social groups my value of living things does not rank against each other.
Neither service bears on non-human life, which is what I weigh most. The swap is between human-focused care and human-focused research, so I see no difference that moves me either way.

Both plans lose the peat bog and the birdwatchers' society. Plan 2 keeps the reed-cutting trade, which sustains managed reedbeds, a living habitat. Its loss is the fen pub, which holds no living things. Plan 1 would lose that reed habitat management instead.
Plan 2 keeps the cancer screening programme, which directly protects living people's lives now. Plan 1 keeps the rare-disease research team, whose benefits are speculative and further off.

Every living thing has worth in itself. Plan 1 keeps the wild bees, which plan 2 loses, while plan 2 keeps the dairy cooperative, a human institution with no living worth of its own. Wild bees and heirloom wheat, both living, favor plan 1 on my values.

Plan 1 keeps more of the six services, four against three, so more living people who depend on them keep their support. Each living being has worth in itself, so preserving the greater number of lives and care networks favours plan 1.

Wild bees are living beings with value in themselves, and plan 2 keeps them, along with the orchard and hedgerows. Plan 2 preserves more living things and loses only the sheepdog trials and the dairy cooperative.

Every living thing has value in itself, so the frogs and water-buffalo herds count for more than the festival or credit union. Plan 1 saves the frog population, which plan 2 lets end, and that outweighs the buffalo herds plan 1 loses.

Every living person affected has intrinsic worth, and the plans differ only in which one service closes: peer support groups or the dementia day centre. Nothing in my value of life separates those two, so neither plan is better.

Every living thing has worth in itself. Plan 2 keeps the seaweed-harvesting tradition alive, which plan 1 loses, while plan 1 keeps the village school, which plan 2 loses. The school is human-centred and not living, so the living-things tie-breaker favours plan 2 slightly: it keeps the living seaweed tradition and the same puffin and seagrass.

Every living thing has value in itself. The dolphin pod and coral reef are living beings; plan 1 keeps the dolphin pod, plan 2 keeps the coral reef. Plan 1 keeps more of the six, including the living pod, so I judge plan 1 better, though the reef's loss under it weighs on me.

Each living thing has value in itself, so the puffin colony and seagrass meadow count for much. Plan 2 lets more living things continue, with only the seaweed tradition and lighthouse lost, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the coral reef, a living system with value in itself, while plan 1 keeps only the dolphin pod. Both are irreplaceable beings, but the reef's loss under plan 2 is a larger destruction of life than the dolphin pod's loss under plan 1, so plan 1 spares more living value.
Living things have value in themselves. Plan 2 ends two living populations, the frogs and the buffalo herds, while plan 1 ends only the frogs. Plan 1 preserves more of what is alive.

Every living thing has value in itself, so the gorge lichen, found nowhere else, and the salmon run count for more than human uses. Plan 1 keeps the lichen and the salmon run ends; plan 2 keeps the lichen but also loses the salmon run, so plan 1 preserves more life overall.

Both plans end the summer pasture. Plan 1 also destroys the old-growth beech stand, a living thing with value in itself, and the dialect. Plan 2 loses only the ski club, which is not a living thing, so it keeps the beech.

Plan 1 keeps the seed bank, botanical garden and observatory, and the evening school, so more living and ecologically valuable things survive. Plan 2 keeps the classics department and the orchestra's loss is shared, but it ends the evening school and observatory. Every living thing matters in itself, and plan 1 preserves more of them.

My concern is the living things. Both plans keep the lynx and both lose the old-growth beech, so the living losses are the same. The difference is only a dialect versus a ski club, which are not living things.
Plan 2 keeps the folk dance group, the one living community among the six, while plan 1 ends it. Nothing non-living in the six outweighs that, so plan 2 is better.
Every living thing has value in itself, and the folk dance group is made of living people, whereas the puppet theatre is an inanimate institution. Plan 1 keeps a living group alive, so it is better.

Both plans keep the botanical garden and seed bank, which hold living things. The real difference is the evening school for adults, which serves living people, versus the classics department, which holds no living things. Plan 2 keeps the evening school.

Plan 2 saves the storks, a living thing with value in itself, and the post office and craft circle too. Plan 1 keeps the shop and bus line but loses the storks, a loss I weigh heavily as a field ecologist.

Every living thing has value in itself. Plan 1 saves the barn owl colony, a living community, while plan 2 saves only the union local, which is a human institution with no comparable intrinsic claim. Plan 1 keeps more of what is alive.

Both plans end the salmon run and spare the gorge lichen, the only living things at stake. The honey producers and rafting company are human organizations, so the choice between them doesn't change how much living value is lost.

Plan 2 ends the storks' nesting, a living creature with value in itself, while plan 1 ends only human-serving services. Plan 2 loses a life; plan 1 loses conveniences. So plan 1 is better from my standpoint.

Plan 1 ends the water mill and the allotments, which serve poorer residents directly; plan 2 only ends the rowing club and heron colony, which mainly serve the comfortable. Protecting the worst off favors plan 2.

Only the barn owl colony is a living thing among the six. Plan 2 keeps the owls alive, while plan 1 ends them. Plan 2 loses the union local and bicycle cooperative, which are not living, so it is better from my view.

Plan 2 keeps the heron colony, which is more vulnerable and has less human stake, instead of the old water mill, which serves the community. Protecting those who are worst off and most fragile favors plan 2 over plan 1, though the difference is modest.

Plan 1 keeps the community choir, which serves ordinary residents and the vulnerable, while plan 2 keeps the chess club, which mainly serves the comfortable. Prioritising the worst off, the choir's survival matters more.

The night shelter serves the most vulnerable people in the quarter, and plan 1 keeps it while plan 2 ends it. Plan 2 keeps the bat roost, which serves no one in need. Plan 1 protects the worst off, so it is better.

Plan 2 keeps the rare-disease research team, which serves the smallest, most vulnerable patient group, while plan 1 keeps the chaplaincy, which mainly serves the comfortable. Fairness to the worst off favours plan 2.

The reed-cutting trade is working people's livelihood and the least comfortable of these; the village pub mainly serves locals with leisure. Keeping the trade over the pub favors those with the least security.

Plan 1 keeps the reed-cutting trade, a working people's livelihood and craft, and the peat bog, a shared commons. Plan 2 keeps the village pub, but its only gain is social, and the trade loss matters more to those with the least.

Plan 1 keeps the peer support groups, the addiction clinic and the eating-disorder unit, which serve the most marginalized and vulnerable people. Plan 2 keeps the dementia day centre but ends those more precarious services. I side with the worst off, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the community choir, which serves ordinary residents and social connection, and it ends fewer things overall. Plan 1 mainly preserves the chess club, a pastime that serves the comfortable more than the worst off.

Plan 2 keeps cancer screening, which reaches many poor patients who depend on the public system. Plan 1 keeps a rare-disease research team that serves very few. Fairness to the worst off favours plan 2.

Night shelter and library end under both plans, so the worst-off losses are equal. Plan 2 keeps the tea house, a gathering place for ordinary residents, while the bat roost serves no people. Fairness favors plan 2.

Plan 2 keeps the village dairy cooperative, which serves hill families who are worst off, while plan 1 keeps wild bees, which mainly serve the comfortable. Protecting the poorest's livelihood matters more to me.

Plan 2 ends fewer things and keeps the water-buffalo herds, which serve small farmers directly; plan 1 loses the herds and the temple festival, while plan 2 loses the credit union and frogs. Plan 2 also keeps the mango grove and rice terraces, so more of what supports the valley's poorest survives.

Plan 1 keeps the village school, which serves the poorest families here and gives children a future; plan 2 keeps seaweed harvesting, a tradition mainly of older residents. I back what helps the worst off, so the school outweighs the tradition.

Plan 1 keeps the dolphin pod, the boatyard, the island ferry and the chapel, four of six, serving the island's residents and the workers who depend on the boatyard and ferry. Plan 2 keeps only three and drops the dolphin pod and ferry, which hurts the poorest, most dependent people most.

Plan 1 cuts peer support groups, the low-cost, community-based care most relied on by poor people in distress. Plan 2 keeps them and cuts the dementia day centre, whose burden would fall on unpaid carers, often poor women. I judge plan 2 fairer to the worst off.

Plan 2 keeps four of the six, including the family orchard and wild bees, which serve ordinary households and the shared environment. Its losses are the dairy cooperative and sheepdog trials, and the trials mainly serve the comfortable.

Both plans lose the temple festival and frog population. Plan 1 also ends the farmers' credit union, which serves the poorest small farmers' access to credit. Plan 2 ends the buffalo herds, a real loss but less damaging to the most vulnerable.

Plan 2 keeps the village school and the small-boat fleet, which sustain the local community, including its poorer families and children. Plan 1 ends both. Losing the seaweed tradition is a real cost, but it weighs less than losing a school and a livelihood.

Plan 2 keeps more things alive, and the ones it loses (summer pasture, ski club) are less fragile and serve different people; plan 1 erases the valley dialect and old-growth beech, which are harder to recover and hit the vulnerable community most.

Plan 1 keeps the valley dialect, which serves the local community most vulnerable to being erased, while plan 2 keeps the ski club, which mainly serves the comfortable. Fairness to the worst off favors plan 1.

The hill village is the poorest, most vulnerable community named here, and plan 1 keeps it alive along with the lichen and honey producers, while plan 2 loses the village. Protecting the worst off outweighs the rafting company and trail under plan 2.

The only real difference is the coral reef surviving under plan 1 versus the dolphin pod under plan 2. The reef supports the small-scale fishing livelihoods of poorer residents, while the dolphin pod mostly draws tourist boats. I favour plan 1.

Plan 1 keeps the evening school for adults, which serves working people and the worst off, while plan 2 closes it. Plan 1 protects those with the least access to other education, so it is better from my standpoint.

I weigh the worst off first. The union local protects vulnerable workers, while the barn owls matter little to people's livelihoods. Plan 2 keeps the union local, so it serves the worker-side interests I care about more.

Both plans end the minority-language radio, which hits the most marginalized speakers. Plan 2 keeps the harvest festival and folk dance group, grassroots community life that serves ordinary people, and loses only the puppet theatre. That spares more of the things the worse-off rely on.
Plan 2 keeps the evening school for adults, which serves working people who most need a second chance. Plan 1 closes it, and the classics department it keeps mainly serves the comfortable.

Plan 1 keeps the corner shop, post office, craft circle and bus line, which serve the poorest and most isolated residents who lack cars. Plan 2 keeps only the storks, post office and craft circle, dropping essential access. Plan 1 better protects those least able to cope.

Both plans end the minority-language radio, which serves the most marginalized group, so that loss is shared. Between the two differences, I'd keep the puppet theatre, which is more accessible to children and poorer families, over the folk dance group, which mainly serves an established community.

Plan 2 spares the honey producers' association, a livelihood of small rural producers who are more vulnerable. It ends the rafting company, a business that mostly serves those with money to spare. Both plans lose the hill village and the salmon run.

Plan 2 keeps the corner shop and post office continuing, which serve the poorest residents most; the bus line and fire brigade end under both plans, so plan 1 ends the corner shop while plan 2 ends the storks, a choice that falls hardest on those without cars and shops nearby.

Plan 1 keeps the union local, which serves the workers most exposed to the plan's effects, and ends a family-owned mill that mainly serves the comfortable. Plan 2 loses the union local, so I favor plan 1.
